item.title: Chest: Efficacy and Safety of Ulinastatin in the Treatment of Patients with Sepsis: The ADJUST Trial
item.description:
Background: Urinary trypsin inhibitor (ulinastatin, UTI) has shown potential survival benefits in sepsis; however, conclusive clinical evidence is lacking.

Research question: In patients with sepsis, does adjunctive ulinastatin, compared with placebo, reduce 28-day all-cause mortality?

Study design and methods: In this multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, adult ICU patients with sepsis meeting Sepsis-3 criteria within 48 hours of admission were randomized (1:1) to receive intravenous UTI (400,000 IU every 8 hours) or placebo, for up to 10 days in addition to standard care. Randomization was stratified by site and septic shock. The primary endpoint was 28-day all-cause mortality. Secondary endpoints included ICU, hospital, and 90-day mortality, and ICU/hospital length of stay.

Results: Of 347 patients randomized, 340 (169 UTI, 171 placebo) received intervention and were included in the safety analysis; after 5 post-intervention withdrawals, 335 (165 UTI, 170 placebo) were included in the intention-to-treat analysis. At 28 days, death had occurred in 39 of 165 patients (23.6%) in the UTI group and in 39 of 170 patients (22.9%) in the placebo group (absolute difference, 0.7% [95% CI -8.4% to 9.7%]; P = .98; hazard ratio 1.03, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.61, P = .90). Secondary outcomes were similar in the two groups. Adverse events occurred in 56.8% (96/169) of UTI and 42.7% (73/171) of placebo patients (absolute difference 14.1%, 95% CI 3.6%-24.6%; P = 0.009).

Interpretation: In patients with sepsis, adjunctive UTI did not reduce mortality compared with placebo. Routine use of UTI for sepsis is not supported by these findings.

Clinical trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov; https://clinicaltrials.gov; NCT02647554.

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Impact of MRSA nasal PCR in the emergency department on duration of vancomycin and linezolid for pneumonia
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Introduction: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a common cause of nosocomial pneumonia, often prompting empiric anti-MRSA therapy despite low prevalence in emergency department (ED) presentations. MRSA nasal polymerase chain reaction (PCR) offers a rapid, non-invasive method to guide de-escalation of MRSA-targeted therapy. This study aims to evaluate the impact of pharmacist-driven MRSA nasal PCR ordering in the ED on the duration of anti-MRSA therapy.

Methods: We conducted a quasi-experimental non-equivalent control study at a single academic center using data from an electronic health record. Adult ED patients with suspected pneumonia who received anti-MRSA therapy in the ED and were subsequently admitted were included. Emergency department pharmacists were responsible for ordering MRSA nasal PCR in compliance with a pre-existing hospital protocol. ED nurses facilitated MRSA nasal PCR collection in the ED.

Results: A total of 200 patients were included in the final analysis. The median duration of anti-MRSA therapy was 5.90 h and 1.13 h for pre- and post-intervention groups, respectively (p = 0.006). Incidence of MRSA nasal PCRs ordered increased from 69.4% pre-intervention to 86.3% post-intervention (p = 0.18). Median length of hospital stay was not significantly different between groups (5.0 days vs. 6.0 days, p = 0.10).

Conclusions: Pharmacist-driven MRSA nasal PCR ordering in the ED significantly reduced anti-MRSA therapy duration without adversely affecting 30-day readmission rates or all-cause 30-day mortality. These findings highlight the value of pharmacist engagement in antibiotic stewardship in the ED.

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Administered opioids and benzodiazepines and the interpretation of positive trauma urine drug screens
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Urine drug screening (UDS) is routine in trauma care, and results populate trauma registries, quality review, and research. Trauma patients receive opioids and benzodiazepines before urine is collected, so a positive class-matched screen may reflect administered drug rather than pre-injury use. We estimated the magnitude of this effect by drug class and its impact on reported prevalence.

Methods: Retrospective cohort of all trauma patients at a Level II center, 2023-2024 (n = 2538), of whom 1420 (55.9%) underwent UDS. Medication administration was matched to the corresponding immunoassay channel, with fentanyl analyzed against its dedicated assay and opiate-assay-matched opioid against the opiate assay. Logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, Injury Severity Score, activation, intubation, and substance use disorder. Treatment-associated positives were estimated by g-computation with bootstrap confidence intervals; cannabinoids, amphetamines, and cocaine were negative controls.

Results: Class-matched positivity greatly exceeded unexposed positivity: 70.0% versus 12.5% for the fentanyl assay (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 15.3, 95% CI 11.5-20.4), 59.0% versus 19.0% for the opiate assay given an opiate-assay-matched opioid (aOR 5.9), and 51.6% versus 8.9% for benzodiazepines (aOR 6.1). Restricting exposure to pre-hospital administration, which necessarily precedes collection, preserved the effect (fentanyl aOR 19.9). Negative controls showed minimal association (amphetamine aOR 1.1). By g-computation, an estimated 62.8% (56.9-68.6) of fentanyl-assay positives, 33.7% of opiate positives, and 29.3% of benzodiazepine positives were associated with administered drug. Any-positive prevalence was 64.4% overall and 37.3% among patients given neither class.

Conclusions: Administered fentanyl was associated with a model-estimated majority of positive fentanyl-assay screens; administered opiates and benzodiazepines were associated with smaller shares of their corresponding positive screens. Class-matched results should be interpreted alongside the medication record. These findings do not establish the source or analytical validity of an individual positive result.

item.title: J Emerg Med: Traumatic Left Main Coronary Artery-Left Anterior Descending Artery Dissection in an Adolescent: A Case Report
item.description:
Background: In adolescents with high-energy blunt chest trauma, electrocardiography (ECG) findings suggestive of myocardial infarction together with markedly elevated cardiac enzymes should raise immediate suspicion for traumatic coronary artery dissection (TCAD).

Case report: We report the case of a 16-year-old male who sustained blunt chest trauma in an electric bicycle accident. During venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) support, non-ECG-gated contrast-enhanced chest computed tomography (CT) was performed. Thin-slice (1.25 mm) delayed-phase images incidentally revealed a double-lumen sign from the left main coronary artery to the proximal left anterior descending artery, along with diffuse myocardial hypoperfusion. These findings prompted angiographic confirmation and urgent coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). WHY SHOULD AN EMERGENCY PHYSICIAN BE AWARE OF THIS?: This case highlights that, in hemodynamically unstable trauma patients, when ECG-gated coronary computed tomography angiography (CTA) is not feasible, careful evaluation of routinely obtained contrast-enhanced CT images, particularly coronary root morphology and myocardial perfusion, may provide critical diagnostic clues to this life-threatening condition.

item.title: J Emerg Med: Comparative Efficacy and Safety of Intranasal Opioids vs. Intravenous Morphine for Acute Moderate-to-Severe Pain: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
item.description:
Background: Intranasal (IN) opioids may provide noninvasive analgesia without delays associated with intravenous (IV) access, but their efficacy and safety vs. IV morphine remain uncertain.

Objectives: To synthesize randomized evidence comparing IN opioids with IV morphine for acute moderate-to-severe pain.

Methods: PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to May 2026 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in adults or children with acute moderate-to-severe pain in emergency, prehospital, procedural, or postoperative settings. Eligible trials directly compared IN opioids with IV morphine. The primary outcome was change in pain score from baseline at 20 and 30 minutes. Secondary outcomes included rescue analgesia and adverse events. Outcomes were pooled as standardized mean differences (SMD) or risk ratios (RR) using random-effects models.

Results: Ten RCTs involving 1164 participants were included. IN opioids showed comparable analgesic efficacy to IV morphine at 20 minutes (SMD = -0.05, 95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.24 to 0.14; p = 0.59; I² = 11.94%) and 30 minutes (SMD = -0.05, 95% CI: -0.24 to 0.15; p = 0.64; I² = 0.00%). Rescue analgesia was comparable (RR = 1.00, 95% CI: 0.81-1.25; p = 0.98). No significant differences were observed in overall adverse events, serious adverse events, respiratory complications, hypotension, gastrointestinal events, dizziness, or rhinorrhea. Dysgeusia was borderline increased.

Conclusion: IN opioids provide analgesic efficacy comparable to IV morphine at 20 and 30 minutes, with no clear increase in systemic adverse events. Larger trials should confirm safety for rare serious events and optimize dosing.

item.title: J Emerg Med: Spontaneous Coronary Artery Dissection: An Emergency Medicine-Focused Narrative Review
item.description:
Background: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) is a nontraumatic, noniatrogenic dissection of a coronary artery.

Objective: This narrative review provides emergency clinicians with a focused overview of the presentation, evaluation, and management of SCAD.

Discussion: SCAD is an underrecognized and potentially deadly disease that can result in coronary artery occlusion and acute coronary syndrome (ACS). It traditionally affects young-to-middle aged females, with increased risk in the peripartum period. Patients with SCAD most commonly present with signs and symptoms consistent with ACS, and a significant proportion of patients will have ST elevation myocardial infarction on electrocardiogram. Emergent cardiology consultation for angiography is necessary for diagnosis. Following diagnosis, a conservative approach is often followed, as most lesions heal spontaneously without intervention. Revascularization in the form of percutaneous coronary artery intervention or coronary artery bypass grafting is necessary in those with ongoing or recurrent ischemia with electrocardiogram or troponin changes, hemodynamic instability, ventricular dysrhythmias, or dissection of the left main coronary artery. Patients can have recurrence of SCAD, and noninvasive imaging modalities, such as coronary computed tomography, may be considered to diagnose recurrence.

Conclusions: Emergency physicians should consider SCAD in patients presenting with ACS, particularly younger women and those without traditional cardiovascular risk factors. Early recognition and prompt consultation with cardiology to guide selection of conservative vs. revascularization strategies are essential to optimize patient outcomes.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Drug Therapies and Incidence of Dementia Among Adults With Overactive Bladder
item.description:
Importance: Concern that anticholinergic medications for overactive bladder (OAB) are associated with increased dementia risk has encouraged a shift toward β3 adrenergic agonists, which are presumed cognitively safer. Whether this presumption is justified is uncertain.

Objective: To compare the risk of incident dementia among adults initiating high-risk anticholinergic, low-risk anticholinergic, or β3 agonist therapy for OAB and to evaluate the association of treatment duration with risk.

Design, setting, and participants: This retrospective cohort study used Epic Cosmos electronic health record data from 2012 to 2025. Adults aged 40 to 90 years newly treated for OAB within 1 year of diagnosis without preexisting dementia were included.

Exposures: First prescribed medication class: high-risk anticholinergics (oxybutynin, tolterodine, or solifenacin), low-risk anticholinergics (darifenacin, trospium, or fesoterodine), or β3 agonists (mirabegron or vibegron).

Main outcomes and measures: Incident dementia by diagnosis code or dementia-specific medication. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) and Cox proportional hazards models were used, with analyses stratified by age and sex and an exploratory landmark duration-response analysis.

Results: Among 830 393 patients (585 198 female [70.5%]; median [IQR] age, 67 [57-76] years), incident dementia occurred in 65 134 patients, with a median (IQR) follow-up ranging from 1046 (571-1809) days for β3 agonists to 1568 (857-2614) days for high-risk anticholinergics. After IPTW, high-risk anticholinergics were associated with a lower hazard of dementia than β3 agonists (hazard ratio [HR], 0.90; 95% CI, 0.87-0.93) and low-risk anticholinergics (HR, 0.93; 95% CI, 0.90-0.96); low-risk anticholinergics did not differ from β3 agonists (HR, 0.97; 95% CI, 0.93-1.01). Weighted 10-year dementia risk was highest for β3 agonists (20.0%; 95% CI, 18.8%-21.2%) and lowest for high-risk anticholinergics (18.1%; 95% CI, 17.9%-18.3%). E-values of 1.29 (high-risk anticholinergics vs β3 agonists) and 1.20 (high-risk vs low-risk anticholinergics) suggested that observed differences could be explained by a modest amount of unmeasured confounding. Longer anticholinergic duration was not associated with increased risk.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of patients undergoing treatment for OAB, β3 agonists were not associated with a lower dementia incidence compared with anticholinergics. These findings suggest that previously reported increases in risk may reflect residual confounding rather than a pharmacological effect.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: A Scalable Teacher Professional Development and Wellness Program in Primary Schools: A Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: In Uganda and other low-income settings with prevalent mental health problems and limited resources, scalable professional development (PD) models are needed to strengthen teachers' capacity to apply evidence-based practices to support child mental health.

Objective: To examine the short-term effectiveness of PD and PD with a teacher-wellness enhancement (PDT) compared with a control condition on teacher knowledge and use of evidence-based practices, teacher stress, and teacher stress management; implementation outcomes; and the differential outcomes between urban and rural primary schools in Uganda.

Design, setting, and participants: This cluster randomized clinical trial was conducted in 47 urban and rural schools in Uganda between August 2021 and February 2025. Participating teachers in the schools were followed-up 24 months after the intervention, and the present trial focused on short-term teacher outcomes. Statistical analysis followed the intention-to-treat principle.

Interventions: Schools and teachers were randomized to 1 of 3 conditions: PD, PDT, and control. The PD intervention (mWEL-PD or Mental Wellbeing and Empowering Lives of the School Community: Professional Development) consisted of 3 days of training and 8 one-hour coaching sessions in person for 2 to 3 months. The PDT intervention (mWEL-PD with a teacher-wellness enhancement) was provided as the PD program plus a 1-day workshop and 3 group support sessions. The control condition offered no intervention during year 1, but mental health knowledge and promotion materials and a 1-day teacher-wellness workshop were provided in year 2.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcomes for PD and PDT groups were knowledge and use of evidence-based practices. Teachers completed 15 self-report measures assessing 4 key outcomes: knowledge of evidence-based practices, use of evidence-based practices, teacher stress, and teacher stress management. Implementation outcomes, self-assessed after completion of the intervention, included teacher engagement in the intervention, teacher perception of acceptability and usefulness of the content, and teacher perception of the competence of the program facilitators.

Results: A total of 47 schools with 509 teachers (mean [SD] age, 40.60 [11.12] years; 368 females [72.3%]) were included in the analysis. Among the schools, 15 (31.9%) were randomly assigned to the control, 16 (34.0%) to the PD, and 16 (34.0%) to the PDT groups. Among teachers, 165 (32.4%) were randomly assigned to the control, 187 (36.7%) to the PD, and 157 (30.8%) to the PDT groups. Teacher attendance at training and coaching sessions and ratings of relevance and facilitator competence were high in both urban and rural contexts. Compared with teachers in the PD group, those in the PDT group were more likely to attend all training days offered (120 of 187 [64.1%] in the PD group vs 127 of 157 [80.9%] in the PDT group) and participated in more coaching sessions (mean [SD] number, 4.58 [2.91] vs 6.09 [2.28]). Compared with teachers in the control condition, teachers in the PDT condition benefited on all 4 key outcomes: increased knowledge (standardized mean difference [SMD], 0.57; 95% CI, 0.26-0.88) and use (SMD, 0.36; 95% CI, 0.01-0.71) of evidence-based practices, increased stress management (SMD, 0.50; 95% CI, 0.19-0.80), and decreased stress (SMD, -0.27; 95% CI, -0.54 to 0.01). Benefits of PD were limited to knowledge of evidence-based practices (SMD, 0.33; 95% CI, 0.03-0.62).

Conclusions and relevance: This trial of a scalable teacher PD program delivered through existing educational infrastructure and resources demonstrates the program's feasibility, acceptability, and impact on self-reported teacher outcomes. The finding of short-term benefits for teacher practice and wellness suggests the potential of the PDT model for school-based mental health promotion.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04383327.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Magnetic Resonance Imaging and Mammography Outcomes by Advanced Breast Cancer Risk
item.description:
Importance: Few studies have examined advanced breast cancer rates in women undergoing routine mammography and/or breast magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

Objective: To compare screening outcomes of breast MRI vs mammography by advanced breast cancer risk and screening round.

Design, setting, and participants: This cohort study included women aged 40 to 74 years who had a screening MRI performed with or without a screening film, digital, or digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) mammogram within 12 months (MRI group) or a screening digital or DBT mammogram (mammography-only group) performed at breast imaging facilities participating in the Breast Cancer Surveillance Consortium (BCSC) between January 1, 2005, and December 31, 2021, and breast cancers diagnosed between January 1, 2005, and December 31, 2022. Data analysis was performed from April 2025 to August 2026.

Exposures: MRI and mammography; advanced breast cancer risk score calculated using the BCSC advanced cancer risk model and categorized as low (0% to <0.172%), average (0.172% to <0.3797%), intermediate (0.3797% to <0.6582%), or higher (≥0.6582%).

Main outcomes and measures: Advanced (prognostic stage II or higher) and screen-detected early-stage (prognostic stage I) invasive cancer and false-positive biopsy recommendation rates per 1000 examinations adjusting for registry, examination year, age, race and ethnicity, family history, prior breast biopsy, and breast density.

Results: A total of 172 865 examinations performed in 105 532 women (median [IQR] age, 52 [46-59] years) were studied. After mammography, the intermediate to high vs low to average risk group had significantly higher advanced cancer (0.6 vs 0.3; difference, 0.4; 95% CI, 0.1-0.6), screen-detected early-stage cancer (2.8 vs 1.8; difference, 1.1; 95% CI, 0.5-1.7), and false-positive biopsy recommendation (18.1 vs 14.7; difference, 3.4; 95% CI, 1.7-5.2) rates per 1000 examinations. In the MRI group, rates per 1000 examinations of advanced cancer (0.8 vs 1.1; difference, -0.3; 95% CI, -1.3 to 0.7), screen-detected early-stage disease (10.3 vs 11.4; difference, -1.1; 95% CI, -4.9 to 2.7), and false-positive biopsy recommendation (94.0 vs 93.3; difference, 0.7; 95% CI, -9.9 to 11.3) were not significantly different between intermediate to high and low to average advanced cancer risk groups. Advanced cancer rates were not significantly different for MRI vs mammography between risk groups (difference, 0.6; 95% CI, -0.4 to 1.6). Screen-detected early-stage rates were significantly higher for MRI vs mammography for low to average risk (11.4 vs 1.8; difference, 9.6; 95% CI, 7.3-12.0) and intermediate to high risk (10.3 vs 2.8; difference, 7.5; 95% CI, 4.9-10.1) groups as were false-positive biopsy recommendation rates for low to average risk (93.3 vs 14.7; difference, 78.6; 95% CI, 72.5-84.8) and intermediate to high risk (94.0 vs 18.1; difference, 75.9; 95% CI, 68.3-83.5) groups. Women who underwent subsequent vs first MRIs had significantly lower advanced cancer rates (0.4 vs 2.0; difference, 1.6; 95% CI, 0.3-2.8) and higher advanced cancer risk (median [IQR] BCSC advanced cancer risk score, 0.348 [0.238 to 0.490] vs 0.301 [0.213 to 0.429]; P < .001).

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study, intermediate to high advanced breast cancer risk was associated with higher advanced cancer rates with screening mammography. MRI screening was associated with higher screen-detected early-stage cancer rates compared with mammography but not lower advanced cancer rates, except among women who underwent repeat MRIs. These results suggest that women with elevated advanced cancer risk should discuss MRI screening with their physician.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Primary Endocrine Therapy vs Upfront Surgery for Older Women With Estrogen Receptor-Positive Breast Cancer: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
item.description:
Importance: As the population of older women with breast cancer grows, an increasing number are considered for primary endocrine therapy (pET), yet clinicians lack a framework for identifying which patients are appropriate candidates, resulting in reliance on chronologic age and life expectancy rather than tumor biology.

Objective: To evaluate survival and variables associated with response duration for patients treated with pET.

Data sources: PubMed, MEDLINE, Web of Science, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched from inception through March 26, 2026.

Study selection: Randomized clinical trials (RCTs) and non-RCT (observational) cohorts comparing pET with surgery in operable, nonmetastatic, estrogen receptor (ER)-positive breast cancer.

Data extraction and synthesis: Data were extracted independently by 2 reviewers per Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. Hazard ratios (HRs) not directly reported were reconstructed from Kaplan-Meier curves. Randomized clinical trial-derived HRs for overall survival (OS) and breast cancer-specific survival (BCSS) were pooled using a random-effects model, given anticipated heterogeneity across trials spanning 5 decades and differing tumor biology criteria. Observational cohorts were analyzed descriptively, not pooled for comparative survival, given susceptibility to confounding by indication.

Main outcomes and measures: The main outcomes were OS and BCSS (RCTs) assessed using meta-analysis. Time to progression, salvage intervention rates, and variables associated with progression and mortality (observational cohorts) were assessed using descriptive analyses.

Results: Twenty-nine studies (6 RCTs and 23 observational cohorts; 22 821 patients; overall median [IQR] age, 83.1 [77.0-85.0] years) met the inclusion criteria. Patients from RCTs were generally younger (median [IQR] age, 77.0 [75.8-78.0] years) than those from the observational studies (median [IQR] age, 84.0 [81.5-86.0] years). Treatment with pET was not associated with a statistically significant OS difference vs surgery (HR, 1.14; 95% CI, 0.98-1.33), though the point estimate favored surgery. Median time to progression ranged from 19.7 months (range, 13.5-26.0 months) in tumor biology-unselected, tamoxifen-era cohorts to more than 50 months in ER-selected and aromatase inhibitor-treated cohorts. Tumor biology was consistently associated with progression risk.

Conclusions and relevance: This systematic review and meta-analysis of more than 22 000 patients with ER-positive breast cancer found no statistically significant survival difference between pET and upfront surgery. Durable disease control under pET seemed to be concentrated in patients with favorable biology. These findings support a framework incorporating tumor biology and frailty, rather than age alone, to identify candidates for pET.

item.title: Am J Respir Crit Care Med: Development and Validation of a Pre-COPD Score to Predict Incident COPD
item.category: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
item.description:
Rationale: The ability to predict progression from a pre-disease state in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), pre-COPD, to overt COPD remains limited.

Objective: To test the hypothesis that development of COPD can be predicted by characterizing pre-COPD and creating a simple pre-COPD score.

Methods: We identified individuals without airflow obstruction, defined as pre-bronchodilator (BD) forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1)/forced vital capacity (FVC)≥0.70 and ≥lower limit of normal, from the Copenhagen General Population Study (CGPS)(N = 14,506), Copenhagen City Heart Study (CCHS)(N = 8673), and Genetic Epidemiology for COPD (COPDGene) Study(N = 2982). A pre-COPD score was developed in CGPS by assigning 1 point to each of smoking history≥10 pack-years, active smoking, any respiratory symptom, asthma, and pre-BD FEV1/FVC 0.70-0.75, and 4 points for pre-BD FEV1<80% predicted, indicating presence of Preserved Ratio Impaired Spirometry (PRISm), with external validation in CCHS and COPDGene. Participants were followed for 5-10 years for incident COPD, defined as pre-BD FEV1/FVC<0.70 and FEV1<80% predicted.

Measurements and main results: During follow-up, COPD developed in 669 individuals (4.6%) in CGPS, 685 (7.9%) in CCHS, and 367 (12%) in COPDGene. In CGPS, 10-year incidence was 1.5% in the low-risk, 9.3% in the intermediate-risk, 24% in the high-risk, and 42% in the very high-risk category. Corresponding 5-year incidences were 3.7%, 7.3%, 12%, and 25% in CCHS, and 4.1%, 5.3%, 13%, and 31% in COPDGene, respectively. item.title: Crit Care: Early adequate empiric antifungal therapy and 28-day mortality in ICU patients with candidemia: a pooled patient-level analysis of EUROBACT-1 and EUROBACT-2 cohorts
item.description:
Background: The optimal timing of empiric antifungal therapy in patients with suspected candidemia remains uncertain. In practice, many antifungal treatments initiated empirically are eventually found to be unnecessary, exposing patients to potential toxicity, selection of non-albicans Candida species, emergence of resistance, and additional costs. The objective of the study was to evaluate whether adequate empiric antifungal therapy initiated within 2 days after blood culture draw was associated with 28-day mortality.

Methods: We performed a pooled secondary analysis of two prospective worldwide observational cohorts (EUROBACT-1 and EUROBACT-2) including adult patients with Candida bloodstream infection. The exposure was defined as receipt of adequate antifungal therapy within 2 days after blood culture draw. Propensity scores for receiving early adequate antifungal therapy were estimated using prespecified covariates, and inverse probability of treatment weights were applied in a weighted Cox proportional hazards model to assess the association with 28-day mortality. Prespecified subgroup analyses were conducted according to study cohort, Candida species, and presence of hypotension at the time of bloodstream infection. As a sensitivity analysis, a frailty Cox proportional hazards model including a random center effect was performed.

Results: The final study population included 272 patients with candidemia from 158 centers, including 81 from EUROBACT-1 and 191 from EUROBACT-2. One hundred and ten patients received early adequate antifungal therapy and 162 did not. Overall, 38.6% of patients (105/272) died within 28 days, including 40.9% (45/110) in the early adequate therapy group and 37.0% (60/162) in the non-early adequate therapy group. In the weighted Cox model, early adequate antifungal therapy was not significantly associated with 28-day mortality (HR 1.23, 95% CI 0.82-1.83, p = 0.314). Results were consistent across subgroup analyses according to study cohort, Candida species, the presence of hypotension at the time of bloodstream infection, as well as in the frailty Cox sensitivity analysis.

Conclusions: Early adequate antifungal therapy was not independently associated with improved 28-day survival in ICU patients with candidemia. These findings support a more targeted approach to early empirical antifungal treatment and underscore the need to identify patient subgroups most likely to benefit from immediate therapy.

item.title: Chest: The Impact of Undernutrition on Post-Tuberculosis Lung-Function: A Prospective Cohort Study
item.description:
Background: Undernutrition is the leading driver of tuberculosis worldwide, yet its effect on the lungs of people who complete treatment is not well defined.

Research question: Among adults treated for drug-sensitive pulmonary tuberculosis, is undernutrition associated with worse post-treatment lung function, radiographic severity, exercise capacity and respiratory quality of life, and does systemic inflammation mediate that association?

Study design and methods: Adults (≥18 years) with drug-sensitive pulmonary tuberculosis were enrolled at treatment initiation in India. We measured associations of baseline body mass index (BMI), mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC), and premorbid BMI with spirometry, chest radiograph score, six-minute walk distance and St George's Respiratory Questionnaire score. Plasma IFN-γ, TNF-α and IL-6 were measured at baseline and month 2; counterfactual mediation analysis partitioned the effect of undernutrition on lung function into direct and inflammation-mediated components.

Results: Of 156 participants analyzed, 76 (48.7%) had a ventilatory defect; 52 (33.3%) had airflow obstruction and 31 (19.9%) had restrictive spirometry. Each 1 kg/m2 higher baseline BMI was associated with lower odds of any ventilatory defect (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 0.78; 95% CI, 0.67-0.90), and BMI below 16 kg/m2 carried five-fold higher odds than BMI ≥18.5 kg/m2 (aOR, 5.08; 95% CI, 1.76-16.02). MUAC and premorbid BMI showed similar associations. Lower BMI was associated with restrictive spirometry (aOR, 0.74 per kg/m2; 95% CI, 0.59-0.89) but not airflow obstruction (aOR, 0.91; 95% CI, 0.80-1.03). Undernourished participants had higher baseline IL-6, which mediated 32% (FEV1) and 49% (FVC) of the association with impaired lung function.

Interpretation: Undernutrition before and at treatment initiation is a potentially modifiable determinant of post-treatment lung impairment, with systemic inflammation mediating part of the effect. Nutritional assessment belongs in routine tuberculosis care, and nutritional support should be tested to prevent lung-function impairment in tuberculosis survivors.

item.title: Chest: The impact of removing prior authorization for guideline-concordant maintenance inhaled medications for COPD: a population-based cohort study
item.description:
Background: Most patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) do not receive maintenance inhaled therapies in concordance with evidence-based clinical guidelines. Long-acting muscarinic antagonists (LAMA), the recommended first-line therapy, is underused, while inhaled corticosteroids (ICS)/long-acting beta-agonists (LABA) are often used in discordance with clinical guidelines. In July 2020, British Columbia's (BC) universal drug plan removed prior authorization requirements for coverage for LAMA medications and restricted coverage for ICS/LABA.

Research question: What is the impact of this policy change on guideline-concordant maintenance inhaled medication use?

Study design and methods: In a population-based cohort study using provincial administrative health data, we identified patients with COPD using a validated case definition and followed them from January 2019 (18 months pre-policy) to December 2022 (30 months post-policy). Using interrupted time series analysis, we evaluated the monthly proportion of patients filling a prescription for ICS/LABA and LAMA, mean canisters dispensed, proportion of days covered (PDC), rates of ICS/LABA discontinuation, LAMA (re)initiation, and initiating LAMA as first maintenance therapy. We report absolute differences between observed and counterfactual outcomes at study end.

Results: The cohort included 47,583 patients with COPD (mean 71.5 years, 46.5% female, 31.7 months mean follow-up). Thirty months post-policy change, ICS/LABA use decreased by -1.3% (95% CI -2.4, -0.3) and LAMA use increased by 0.8% (95% CI 0.1, 1.6). There was no significant change in the number of ICS/LABA canisters dispensed, PDC or proportion discontinuing ICS/LABA. Mean LAMA canisters dispensed increased by 9.8 per 1,000 patients (95% CI 1.0, 18.7) and PDC increased by 1.5% (95% CI 0.5, 2.4). (Re)initiation of LAMA or initiating LAMA as maintenance therapy increased by 0.2% (95% CI 0.02, 0.3) and 34.8% (95% CI 22.3, 48.6), respectively. Total combined drug costs did not change.

Interpretation: Changes to drug coverage in BC were associated with improved guideline-concordant medication use.

item.title: Chest: Pretransplant Pulmonary Hemodynamics, Explant Histology, and Primary Graft Dysfunction after Lung Transplantation for Silicosis
item.description:
Background: Silicosis associated with progressive massive fibrosis (PMF) is a major cause of end-stage lung disease among workers in the artificial stone industry. Patients with PMF are increasingly referred for lung transplant (LTx) evaluation and there is emerging evidence of pulmonary hypertension (PH) in patients with advanced PMF.

Research question: Among patients with PMF referred for lung transplantation, what is the incidence of PH and what are accompanying histopathologic pulmonary vascular aberrations?

Study design and methods: Retrospective single-center cohort study of prospectively-enrolled participants, providing granular data on the invasive hemodynamic profile of patients with silicosis-associated PMF, histopathologic data on pulmonary vascular aberrations, and clinical data on post-transplant complications. Clinical and sociodemographic variables were collected. Explanted lungs from patients with silicosis-associated PMF underwent detailed pulmonary vascular histopathologic review and were descriptively compared with PAH explants. The incidence of primary graft dysfunction (PGD) was evaluated and descriptive analysis performed to provide associations of clinical features and PGD incidence.

Results: PH was present in over 95% of 21 patients with silicosis-associated PMF who underwent LTx, with a hemodynamic profile similar to patients transplanted for PAH. . Silicosis explants showed confluent silicotic nodules, extensive fibrosis and hyalinization, obscuration or obliteration of vascular structures, and perivascular fibrohistiocytic infiltrates with extrinsic narrowing. Classic PAH-type arteriolar muscular hypertrophy and plexiform arteriopathy were uncommon. In exploratory comparisons, patients who developed PGD had more frequent pretransplant right ventricular dysfunction (71% vs 21%; risk difference 0.50, 95% CI 0.06-0.75) and a lower median TAPSE/RVSP ratio (0.27 vs 0.39; Hedges' g -0.93, 95% CI -1.88 to 0.02) than in those without PGD.

Interpretation: These findings suggest that PH in advanced silicosis with PMF is very common and represents a distinct pulmonary vascular phenotype characterized by extensive fibrotic vascular obliteration rather than the classic arteriopathy seen in PAH.

item.title: Lancet: Eating disorders
item.description:
The eating and feeding disorders are serious psychiatric disorders at the mind-body interface, often with an exceptionally high burden for affected individuals, their families and supporters, and wider society. In anorexia nervosa, high acute medical risk and patients' ambivalence about treatment can make a challenging combination that can impede engagement. First-line treatments for eating disorders are mainly psychological, with medications playing an adjunctive role. Novel biological and technology-based interventions are only slowly emerging. Compared with other psychiatric disorders, research into these disorders is seriously underfunded. Many uncertainties regarding their aetiology, maintenance, and treatment remain. Controversies mainly concern the treatment and care of those with the most severe and longstanding forms of illness. Advances in knowledge are most likely to arise from longitudinal studies combining multimodal assessments, using big data to develop better mechanistic understanding, and greater use of flexible trial designs to allow development of more personalised and precise interventions.

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Association between mechanical ventilation with positive end-expiratory pressure and outcomes in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Aim: The effect of positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) during intermittent positive pressure ventilation in patients undergoing cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) on outcome is unknown. The aim of this study was to evaluate the association between the use of PEEP during cardiopulmonary resuscitation and clinical outcomes in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients.

Methods: We conducted a single-centre observational cohort study using a retrospective analysis of data collected prospectively within a dedicated research registry of adult OHCA patients managed by a physician-staffed prehospital emergency medical team. All included patients were intubated and ventilated either with mechanical ventilation using PEEP or with manual ventilation without PEEP. Intratracheal pressure was continuously recorded via a catheter connected to a portable device, allowing objective verification of PEEP application and ventilation rate. The association between mechanical ventilation with PEEP use and clinical outcomes was evaluated using multivariable logistic regression adjusted for relevant confounders.

Results: 362 patients were included, with a median age of 65 years (54-79), of whom 250 (69.1%) were male. Median ventilation rate was 15 breaths/min (10-19). Of all patients, 149 (41.2%) achieved Return Of Spontaneous Circulation (ROSC) and 31 (8.6%) survived to hospital discharge. The adjusted odds ratio (OR) of mechanical ventilation with PEEP for achieving ROSC was 1.58 (95% CI 1.01-2.50, p = 0.048). The unadjusted OR of mechanical ventilation with PEEP for survival to hospital discharge was 2.22 (95% CI 1.03-4.78; p = 0.037).

Conclusion: The use of mechanical ventilation with PEEP during CPR in OHCA patients was associated with higher likelihood of ROSC.

item.title: Crit Care Med: Long-Term Mortality in Sepsis Survivors: A Population-Based Study During 15 Years
item.description:
Objectives: To evaluate long-term mortality among sepsis survivors in Catalonia over a 15-year period and to identify factors associated with increased mortality within 2 years after hospital discharge.

Design: Retrospective population-based cohort study.

Setting: Acute-care hospitals in Catalonia, Spain.

Patients: Adult and pediatric patients hospitalized with sepsis between 2005 and 2019 identified using the International Classification of Diseases, 9th Revision, Clinical Modification and International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision, Clinical Modification codes for infection and acute organ dysfunction. Patients who died during hospitalization, were transferred to another facility, or represented readmission episodes were excluded.

Interventions: None.

Measurements and main results: Data were obtained from the Catalan Minimum Basic Dataset of Acute-Care Hospitals, with longitudinal follow-up through the Central Registry of Insured Persons. Comorbidities were assessed using the Charlson comorbidity index. Logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards models were used to identify predictors of long-term mortality. Among 296,554 hospital admissions for sepsis, 237,075 patients (79.9%) survived to hospital discharge. Of these, 42% died (99,571) within 2 years. Long-term mortality increased significantly with age, ranging from 5.8% in patients younger than 15 years to 62% in those older than 84 years (p < 0.0001), and with comorbidity burden (21%, 38%, 51%, and 67% for Charlson index 0, 1-2, 3-4, and ≥ 5, respectively; p < 0.0001). Neoplasia (hazard ratio [HR], 2.011), liver cirrhosis (HR, 1.562), and dementia (HR, 1.304) were the comorbidities most strongly associated with mortality. Longer hospital stays were also associated with increased mortality. A progressive decline in long-term mortality was observed during 2017-2019.

Conclusions: Long-term mortality among sepsis survivors remains high, with more than 40% dying within 2 years after hospital discharge. These findings support the need for structured post-sepsis care strategies focused on high-risk patients, improved continuity of care, and prevention of long-term sepsis-related complications.

Objectives: To develop and validate a shorter Family Satisfaction in the ICU (FS-ICU) questionnaire that reduces survey length while preserving content and psychometric performance for quality improvement and benchmarking. The FS-ICU survey assesses family perceptions of care, communication, and decision-making and has been translated into multiple languages with implementation across diverse health care systems internationally. In a province-wide electronic implementation in Ontario, more than 40% of initiated surveys were incomplete, suggesting that survey length may limit practicality for large-scale quality improvement and benchmarking.

Design: Multistage study using provincial FS-ICU survey data and an independent multicenter validation dataset for item reduction, psychometric evaluation, agreement testing, and external validation of a shortened questionnaire.

Setting: A 12-member expert working group, convened for a Critical Care Services Ontario initiative, used provincial web-based data from adult ICUs across Ontario to develop a shorter version, FS-ICUshort. External validation was applied to FS-ICUshort using a separate multicenter Canadian revised FS-ICU dataset.

Participants: A 12-member expert working group led by Dr. Daren K. Heyland, including administrative staff, ICU clinical staff, patient experience specialists, and quality improvement specialists from Ontario, used provincial FS-ICU rollout data.

Interventions: None.

Measurements and main results: Using empirical criteria and expert ratings, the FS-ICU was reduced from 29 to 12 items: seven in the satisfaction-with-care domain (FS-Care) and five in the communication and decision-making domain (FS-DM). FS-ICUshort showed high internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.93 for FS-Care, 0.86 for FS-DM, and 0.94 for total). Confirmatory factor analysis supported a two-factor structure with better fit than a single-factor model. Scores from FS-ICUshort closely matched full FS-ICU, with mean differences less than or equal to 1.1 points on a 0-100 scale and intraclass correlations of 0.97-0.99. External validation replicated these results.

Conclusions: The 12-item FS-ICUshort maintains the core content and psychometric quality of the original FS-ICU while significantly reducing length, supporting routine use in ICU family experience measurement and benchmarking.

item.description:
Importance: Refusal of newborn prophylactic vitamin K has been increasing in the US, placing more infants at risk for vitamin K deficiency bleeding.

Objective: To describe US trends in nonreceipt of newborn vitamin K and infant bleeding, and to compare risks of bleeding and mortality with concurrent bleeding among infants who did and did not receive newborn intramuscular (IM) vitamin K.

Design, setting, and participants: This retrospective cohort study included infants born at 35 to 43 weeks' gestation between January 1, 2017, and December 31, 2025, at hospitals and health systems from 50 states contributing to the Epic Cosmos dataset.

Exposure: Nonreceipt of newborn IM vitamin K.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was bleeding within the first 6 months of life based on International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision codes. Secondary outcomes were bleeding during the birth hospitalization and after discharge, intracranial bleeding, and mortality with concurrent bleeding during the birth hospitalization. Robust Poisson regression was used to estimate relative risks while adjusting for covariates.

Results: Among 5 240 780 infants, the rate of vitamin K nonreceipt increased from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025. Between 2017 and 2025, the incidence of bleeding by 6 months increased from 225.3 to 394.0 per 10 000 births in infants who did not receive newborn IM vitamin K, compared with 136.6 to 221.8 per 10 000 in infants who received vitamin K. Infants who did not receive vitamin K had significantly higher risk of bleeding by 6 months than infants who did receive vitamin K (288.0 vs 185.9 per 10 000; adjusted risk ratio [ARR], 1.47; 95% CI, 1.43-1.51). They also had higher risk of intracranial bleeding (33.0 vs 13.2 per 10 000; ARR, 2.43; 95% CI, 2.26-2.62) and mortality with concurrent bleeding during the birth hospitalization (2.9 vs 1.1 per 10 000; ARR, 2.69; 95% CI, 2.09-3.47).

Conclusions and relevance: Nonreceipt of vitamin K and infant bleeding incidence have increased in the US, and newborns who did not receive vitamin K were at significantly higher risk of bleeding during their first 6 months.

Design, setting, and participants: This cross-sectional study used demographic and health data from January to September 2024 cycles of the nationally representative Household Pulse Survey conducted by the US Census Bureau. Exposure: State-level implementation of SEBT between May and August 2024 (treated vs untreated states).

Main outcomes and measures: Household food insufficiency, measured by a respondent indicating they sometimes or often did not have enough food in their household during the previous 7 days.

Results: Among 31 059 SEBT-eligible households (1090 Asian [3.5%], 5692 Black [18.3%], 5845 Hispanic [18.8%], 21 166 White [68.1%]), the majority of households in both untreated (18 states) and treated (33 states, including District of Columbia) states had income below 185% FPL (10 233 [93.4%] and 17 105 [92.0%], respectively). item.description:
Importance: Molecular evaluation is standard of care for patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) in the US. Patients in rural areas face disproportionate lung cancer mortality associated with reduced guideline-concordant evaluation and treatment receipt, but molecular testing patterns have not been described in this population.

Objective: To characterize molecular testing patterns in the rural US following initial testing implementation.

Design, setting, and participants: This cohort study used the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results Program linked to Medicare claims data to identify individuals aged 66 years or older diagnosed with advanced NSCLC from January 2014 to December 2019. Data analysis was performed from December 2025 to August 2026.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Changes in Racial, Ethnic, and Gender Differences in Promotion and Retention Among US Medical School Clinical Faculty
item.description:
Importance: Understanding how racial-, ethnic-, and gender-based differences in academic promotion have changed over time is important for advancing equity in academic medicine.

Objective: To examine changes over time in racial-, ethnic-, and gender-based differences in promotion and attrition among academic clinical faculty.

Design, setting, and participants: This cohort study used deidentified data from the AAMC faculty roster for full-time faculty appointments between 1960 and 2024, based on an August 31, 2025, data snapshot.

Exposure: Race and ethnicity (categorized as American Indian, Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian, or Pacific Islander; Asian; Black; Hispanic; White; and other [any race or ethnicity not otherwise specified]), gender, and medical school graduation cohort (2000 or earlier vs after 2000).

Main outcomes and measures: Cox proportional hazards models were used to examine differences in promotion to associate professor, professor, and attrition by race, ethnicity, and gender across medical school graduation cohorts and were presented as adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs).

Results: Included were 289 129 physicians at 152 institutions (179 081 men [61.9%]; 1093 American Indian, Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian, or Pacific Islander [0.4%]; 62 403 Asian [21.6%]; 13 330 Black [4.6%]; 16 865 Hispanic [5.8%]; 3034 other [1.1%]; 192 404 White [66.6%]). Compared with White faculty, Black faculty were less likely to be promoted to associate professor overall; this difference narrowed over time (before 2000: aHR, 0.67; 95% CI, 0.60-0.74; after 2000: aHR, 0.77; 95% CI, 0.71-0.83; P for interaction = .01). The difference in promotion to professor between Black and White faculty also narrowed over time (before 2000: aHR, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.77-0.94; after 2000: aHR, 1.09, 95% CI, 0.92-1.29; P for interaction = .02). Women were less likely than men to be promoted to associate professor, although this difference narrowed over time (before 2000: aHR, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.77-0.82; after 2000: aHR, 0.91; 95% CI, 0.85-0.98; P for interaction <.001). Women were less likely than men to be promoted to professor in both graduation cohorts, with no evidence of change over time (before 2000: aHR, 0.93; 95% CI, 0.90-0.97; after 2000: aHR 0.91; 95% CI, 0.83-0.99; P for interaction = .48). Attrition was more likely among American Indian, Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian, or Pacific Islander (aHR, 1.25; 95% CI, 1.12-1.40), Asian (aHR, 1.07; 95% CI, 1.04-1.10), Black (aHR, 1.19; 95% CI, 1.14-1.25), Hispanic (aHR, 1.10; 95% CI, 1.05-1.15), and women (aHR, 1.11; 95% CI: 1.08-1.13) faculty than among White and men faculty.

Conclusions and relevance: In this retrospective cohort study of 289 129 physicians, Black faculty experienced less disparity in promotion over time, and disparities in promotion to associate professor also narrowed for women; however, women remained less likely to be promoted to professor, and attrition remained higher for all minoritized racial and ethnic groups and for women. These findings suggest incremental progress while underscoring the need for continued efforts to achieve greater diversity and equity within academic medicine.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Indoor Radon and Incident Heart Failure Among Postmenopausal Women
item.description:
Importance: Evidence has shown an association of radon exposure with heart failure risk factors, but whether there is an association with heart failure remains unclear.

Objective: To assess whether indoor radon concentrations are associated with incident heart failure among US postmenopausal women.

Design, setting, and participants: This prospective cohort study used data from the Women's Health Initiative (WHI) observational study and clinical trials. Participants were postmenopausal women from 40 US clinical centers who were aged 50 to 79 years and did not have self-reported heart failure at enrollment or randomization (September 1993 to December 1998) but had physician adjudication of heart failure during follow-up through February 17, 2024.

Exposure: Geocoded participant address-based assignment of county-level, US Environmental Protection Agency-categorized indoor radon concentration (<2, 2-4, or >4 picocuries [pCi]/L).

Main outcome and measure: Incident hospitalization for acute decompensated heart failure was ascertained through physician adjudication of medical records. Hazard ratios (HRs) for heart failure by indoor radon concentration were estimated with Cox proportional hazards regression models.

Results: Among 43 188 postmenopausal women (mean [SD] age, 63 [7] years), 36% were exposed to a radon concentration less than 2 pCi/L; 41%, to a concentration of 2 to 4 pCi/L; and 23%, to a concentration of more than 4 pCi/L. Over a mean (SD) follow-up of 16.2 (8.4) years, 3446 incident heart failure events occurred. The fully adjusted HR for heart failure was 1.19 (95% CI, 1.07-1.33) at more than 4 pCi/L vs less than 2 pCi/L, changing little in sensitivity analyses. The HR was higher for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (1.24; 95% CI, 1.04-1.49) and heart failure mortality (1.37; 95% CI, 1.12-1.69) at radon concentrations more than 4 pCi/L vs less than 2 pCi/L, but these HRs were not different from the null at concentrations of 2 to 4 pCi/L vs less than 2 pCi/L. The HR at concentrations greater than 4 pCi/L approximated that of a 16-mm Hg increase in systolic blood pressure or an increase of 4.8 in body mass index (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared).

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of US postmenopausal women, higher indoor radon concentrations were associated with an increased risk of incident heart failure, suggesting that radon may be a modifiable environmental determinant of heart failure.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Distribution of Coal Power, Pollution, and Poverty
item.description:
Importance: The adverse social exposome-life-course exposure to harmful social-environmental conditions-is associated with poor health outcomes. Exposure to heavy metals in air pollution from coal-fired power plants (CPP) may represent an underlying mechanism of this disparity, yet the association between the US adverse social exposome measured with the Area Deprivation Index (ADI) and CPP remains unknown.

Objective: To characterize the populations and adverse social exposome (indexed by ADI) of communities neighboring operational CPP.

Design, setting, and participants: Cross-sectional study of the US population using data from the 2023 Neighborhood Atlas. Data were analyzed from March to April 2026.

Exposure: Proximity to CPP was operationalized using 4 circular buffer zones: 3, 10, 25, and 50 miles in radius.

Main outcomes and measures: (1) Characterize each buffer zone by ADI and (2) determine the potential population-level exposure to CPP. Census block group delineations and population characteristics are from time-concordant US Census and American Community Survey data.

Results: The 2023 US population included 335 563 144 people (169 517 541 [50.5%] female, 66 294 296 [19.8%] Hispanic, 269 268 846 [80.2%] not Hispanic or Latino, and 212 002 396 [63.1%] White). A total of 2 783 004 people (0.83% of the US population) lived within 3 miles of a CPP. This group was more likely to live in the highest ADI neighborhoods as compared with the lowest ADI neighborhoods. Compared with the US population, these individuals were more likely to be American Indian and Alaska Native, White, and non-Hispanic. Populations living in the lowest 10% of ADI neighborhoods (most advantaged) had lower odds (odds ratio, 0.04; 95% CI, 0.00-0.81) of living within 3 miles of a CPP as compared with populations living in the highest 10% of ADI neighborhoods (most disadvantaged).

Conclusions and relevance: In this cross-sectional study of US communities' proximity to CPP, we found that neighborhoods potentially exposed to CPP's hazardous environmental toxicants were more likely to be high ADI (ie, lower socioeconomic status) than low ADI (ie, higher socioeconomic status), highlighting the significantly greater burden of environmental toxicants potentially borne by disadvantaged US populations. Recent federal deregulations are likely to further increase these potential CPP-related toxin exposures. Additional study is needed to determine if these environmental toxicants trigger biological mechanisms underpinning the association between high ADI and poor health.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: US Medical Education Reform Reports, 1910 to 2024
item.description:
Importance: Since the early 20th century, prominent private foundations, medical organizations, and government agencies have published reports calling for reform of medical education; however, it is unclear whether these reports contain repetitive messages about improving medical education, are a source of curriculum improvement, and are an antidote to medical education inertia.

Objective: To replicate and amplify findings of a similar analysis of reports published between 1910 and 1993 that advocated for reform in medical education using reports published from 1995 to 2024 and to identify recurring themes and potential sources of inertia in medical education.

Evidence review: PubMed, Scopus, Education Resources Information Center, and Google were searched on February 4, February 13, and March 19, 2025, using search terms addressing medical education, reform, and recommendations to identify reports on reform in medical education. A descriptive and interpretive content analysis of the medical education reports spanning 114 years was conducted from February 2025 to May 2026.

Findings: A total of 47 reports, including 19 analyzed in the previous study, were identified and analyzed. Consistent coding of content in the 47 reports was achieved. One of 4 core reform objectives of medical education, serve changing public interest, increased in endorsement over time. The other 3 core objectives-address physician workforce needs, cope with burgeoning knowledge, foster generalism-decreased or were unchanged. Four secondary reform objectives-apply new educational methods, address the changing nature of illness burden, address the changing nature of practice, increase quality and standards of education-increased in prevalence. Proposed methods of educational reform varied over 114 years, shaped by conceptual updates and technology advancements. None of the reports expressed criticism of traditional apprenticeship clinical education. Few reports displayed knowledge or awareness of the science of expertise in medical education.

Conclusions and relevance: In this study of medical education reports issued over 114 years, 3 basic values emerged: reform medical education, affirm core social and professional values, and protect the profession from outside intrusion. Proposed reform objectives and the means to achieve them displayed both stability and change longitudinally. The time-honored apprenticeship approach to clinical education was unquestioned. Despite a growing body of evidence from the science of expertise, proposed medical education reforms have produced insignificant curriculum change.

item.title: Intensive Care Med: Consensus on a core outcome set for ventilation trials in critically ill patients with acute brain injury: results of an international Delphi consensus study
item.description:
Purpose: Clinical research evaluating mechanical ventilation liberation in patients with acute brain injury (ABI) shows substantial outcome heterogeneity, limiting evidence synthesis. We aimed to develop an internationally endorsed core outcome set (COS) and a hierarchical composite endpoint for ventilation trials in neurocritical care.

Methods: Following COS-STAD/COS-STAP standards, we conducted a 4-round international Delphi study. Candidate outcomes were identified via a scoping review. A multidisciplinary panel from 31 countries scored outcomes using a 9-point GRADE scale. Inclusion required >70% rating as "critical" (score 7-9) and ≤15% as "not important" (1-3). Two consensus meetings were held to categorize outcomes, select representative measures, and ratify a hierarchical composite endpoint.

Results: 78 stakeholders participated in Round 1; 60 completed all rounds (23.1% attrition). Fifty-four outcomes achieved Delphi consensus. At Consensus Meeting 1, these were organized into 16 categories; the highest-scoring outcome per category was selected. Three outcomes were not ratified due to disease-specificity (NIH Stroke Scale) or lack of universal applicability (brain death, coma-free days). The final COS comprised 13 outcomes across 5 domains: respiratory function, survival, complications, functional status, and quality of life. A 3-level hierarchical composite endpoint was ratified at Consensus Meeting 2: (1) intensive care unit survival, (2) no reintubation within 72 hours, and (3) days alive without mechanical ventilation.

Conclusion: This study establishes the first COS for ventilation weaning trials in ABI patients. Widespread adoption of these 13 outcomes and the hierarchical composite endpoint will standardize reporting, enable meaningful evidence synthesis, and facilitate clinical translation in neurocritical care.

Trial registration: Core Outcome Measures in Effectiveness Trials (COMET) Initiative, registration number 2320.

item.title: Acad Emerg Med: Geriatric Emergency Management Programs and Days at Home Among People Living With Dementia in Ontario
item.category: Academic emergency medicine : official journal of the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine
item.description:
Background: People living with dementia frequently present to emergency departments (EDs) and are at increased risk of hospitalization, institutionalization, and other adverse outcomes. Geriatric Emergency Management (GEM) programs are designed to improve emergency care for older adults, but their effectiveness among people living with dementia remains uncertain. We evaluated the association between attendance at an ED with an active GEM program and days alive and at home among older adults living with dementia.

Methods: We conducted a population-based retrospective cohort of Ontario residents aged 65 years or older with identified dementia who had an index ED visit between April 1, 2021, and March 31, 2024. The exposure was attendance at an ED with an active GEM program.

Results: The cohort included 145,874 individuals, including 110,288 who presented to EDs with GEM programs and 35,586 who presented to EDs without GEM programs. The median age of the population was 81 years and 58.5% of participants were female. After propensity score overlap weighting and adjustment for facility characteristics, individuals who visited GEM EDs spent 7.5 (95% CI, 3.1-12.0) more days alive and at home during the following year than those who visited non-GEM EDs. Approximately half of this difference was attributable to fewer days spent in long-term care homes. Visits to GEM EDs were also associated with fewer subsequent ED visits, although index ED length of stay and hospital admission rates were higher.

Conclusions and relevance: Among older adults living with dementia, care in EDs with GEM programs was associated with more days alive at home over the following year. These findings support continued investment in GEM programs to promote aging at home and to delay institutionalization among people living with dementia.

item.title: Crit Care: Treatment and outcomes of difficult-to-treat Stenotrophomonas maltophilia pneumonia in the intensive care unit: a multinational retrospective cohort study
item.description:
Objectives: Difficult-to-treat resistance (DTR) in Stenotrophomonas maltophilia is an emerging concern in ICU-acquired pneumonia, associated with high mortality and limited evidence to guide therapy. This study aimed to evaluate the association between antibiotic regimens and 30-day mortality in DTR S. maltophilia ICU-acquired pneumonia.

Methods: We conducted a multicenter, international, retrospective study across 31 centers in eight countries, including all adult patients with DTR S. maltophilia ICU-acquired pneumonia treated with ≥24 hours of an in vitro-active antibiotic. The primary outcome was 30-day mortality. Secondary outcomes included clinical cure and a composite of 30-day survival with clinical cure. Each agent was analyzed as a separate exposure using modified Poisson regression with robust variance in a day-3 landmark cohort. Combination therapy and treatment duration were evaluated using overlap weighting.

Results: A total of 119 patients were included. Thirty-day mortality was 37.8%. Tigecycline was associated with higher 30-day mortality (aRR 1.95, 95% CI 1.21-3.13). Aztreonam/ceftazidime-avibactam showed a favorable but non-significant trend toward lower mortality (aRR 0.38, 95% CI 0.12-1.15), as did colistin (aRR 0.51, 95% CI 0.22-1.20). No agent other than tigecycline was significantly associated with any outcome, and the active agents had wide, overlapping confidence intervals. Neither combination therapy nor a treatment duration longer than 8 days was associated with any outcome.

Conclusions: Tigecycline was associated with excess mortality and should be used with caution. Aztreonam/ceftazidime-avibactam and colistin trended toward lower mortality, whereas the other agents, including cefiderocol, appeared neutral. The study is underpowered to separate the active agents, and these hypothesis-generating findings require prospective confirmation.

item.description:
Background: Down syndrome, also known as Trisomy 21, is the most common chromosomal abnormality causing intellectual disability. The life expectancy for people with Down syndrome has increased considerably over the last few decades, and many of these patients struggle with the transition from pediatric to adult medical care. There is currently no information on how adults with Down syndrome use emergency departments (EDs). The objective of this study was to describe visits by adult patients with Down syndrome to an academic medical center.

Methods: This was a retrospective chart review study of all adult patients (age ≥ 18 years) with Down syndrome who presented to The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center (OSUWMC) EDs from January 1, 2019 to December 31, 2023. Selected patient and visit characteristics were collected by chart review. This was a descriptive study with data presented as n and percentage.

Results: There were 177 ED visits by 106 adults with Down syndrome during the study period. Most patients had a single ED visit (69.8%) and more than half the patients were under age 40 (52.9%). The most common chief complaints were abdominal pain (10.2%) and seizure (7.9%). The majority received laboratory testing (82.5%) and/or imaging (74.6%) This pattern was present across the age span. Most were discharged to place of residence (51.4%) but admission rates were higher (38.4%). Laboratory testing, imaging and admission rates were higher compared to local and national rates.

Conclusions: This description of ED visits by adult patients with Down syndrome provides insight into common presenting complaints, testing patterns, disposition, and post-ED visits. Study data suggest that adult patients with Down syndrome may require different considerations when they present to adult EDs compared to a typical ED patient. Further studies are needed to generalize these results and identify ways to improve their ED care.

item.title: Crit Care: Physiological determinants of piperacillin and cefazolin clearance in septic and trauma patients
item.description:
Background: Physiological alterations in patients with sepsis and trauma can influence antibiotic clearance, yet reliable predictors remain poorly defined. We aimed to investigate the determinants of piperacillin and cefazolin clearance in these populations to identify bedside indicators of subtherapeutic exposure.

Methods: Prospective physiological and pharmacokinetic study in patients receiving piperacillin/tazobactam for sepsis or prophylactic cefazolin post-trauma. Patients also received intravenous sinistrin. Intensive pharmacokinetic sampling, cardiac output (CO) monitoring and four urinary creatinine clearance (uCLCR) measurements were performed. Data were analysed with non-compartmental pharmacokinetic methods, and linear and logistic regression.

Results: We enrolled 49 septic and 28 trauma patients. Trauma patients were younger (33.5 vs. 46.5 years) and had higher uCLCR (155.5 vs. 107.5 mL/min). Linear regression identified that lower Sequential Organ Failure Assessment scores and an hyperdynamic state with higher CO and 2 and 8-h uCLCR were the strongest predictors of increased piperacillin total clearance; higher 2-h uCLCR and hypoalbuminemia were the main predictors for cefazolin total clearance. Sinistrin CL was a weak predictor. Logistic regression identified augmented renal clearance (8-h uCLCR > 130 mL/min) as the main risk factor for piperacillin subtherapeutic exposure (OR 10.9, p < 0.05), also when defined using the Cockcroft-Gault cut-off of 114.5 mL/min from ROC analysis.

Conclusions: In sepsis, low sickness severity and a hyperdynamic state with high cardiac output lead to increased uCLCR and high piperacillin clearance. In trauma, high cefazolin clearance occurs in the presence of an elevated uCLCR and hypoalbuminemia. These bedside physiological indicators, along with Cockcroft-Gault CLCR, may serve as early indicators of risk for subtherapeutic exposure.

item.title: Crit Care: Assessing vascular barrier permeability in critically ill patients: what are we really measuring?
item.description:
Background: Perturbation of vascular barrier permeability is a central mechanism in the pathophysiology of critical illness, contributing to tissue edema, impaired oxygen diffusion, and organ dysfunction. Despite advances in the field, direct bedside assessment of vascular permeability remains unavailable. Current approaches rely on indirect and compartment-specific surrogates, raising important questions about what is actually being measured.

Main body: This narrative review summarizes the physiological principles underlying vascular barrier function and its disruption in conditions such as sepsis, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and major surgery. Currently available bedside tools used to assess vascular permeability or its consequences are critically appraised, including clinical examination, ultrasonography, transpulmonary thermodilution, bioelectrical impedance analysis, circulating biomarkers of endothelial injury (e.g., glycocalyx degradation products, angiopoietin-2), and albumin kinetics-based methods. While these techniques provide valuable insights, they predominantly reflect downstream consequences such as tissue edema, intravascular volume shifts, or endothelial activation rather than permeability itself. In addition, vascular permeability is a dynamic, context-dependent, and organ-specific process influenced by inflammatory, hemodynamic, and therapeutic factors, further complicating its interpretation. Each method therefore captures only a partial dimension of vascular barrier dysfunction, with important limitations related to specificity, feasibility, validation and standardization.

Conclusions: No single bedside tool currently provides a comprehensive assessment of vascular permeability in critically ill patients. A multimodal approach integrating clinical evaluation, imaging, hemodynamic monitoring, and biomarkers is required to better characterize vascular barrier dysfunction. Future research should focus on validating composite indices and developing reliable, real-time bedside tools capable of directly assessing vascular permeability, with the ultimate goal of improving risk stratification and guiding personalized therapeutic strategies.

item.title: Crit Care: Harmonizing the diagnosis of citrate accumulation - a call for standardized criteria
item.description:
Regional citrate anticoagulation (RCA) has emerged as the gold-standard strategy for continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), yet its widespread adoption remains hindered by perceived complexity, heterogeneous protocols, unclear contraindications, and inconsistent terminology. A central challenge lies in the recognition and management of citrate accumulation, for which no single, reliable biomarker exists. The total-to-ionized calcium (tCa/iCa) ratio is widely utilized as a sensitive surrogate, but its specificity is limited by multiple confounding factors, including serum albumin concentration, acid-base status, and exogenous calcium administration. Current evidence supports a paradigm shift from reliance on static thresholds toward a dynamic, physiology-based assessment to define citrate accumulation. The kinetics of the tCa/iCa ratio, when interpreted alongside evolving metabolic parameters, particularly lactate trends, systemic ionized calcium, and acid-base status, provide a more robust framework for identifying citrate accumulation. Crucially, an elevated tCa/iCa ratio should not indiscriminately prompt the discontinuation of RCA. Targeted adjustments to the CRRT prescription can often safely mitigate citrate burden while preserving circuit patency. In the absence of a validated and widely available method for the direct measurement of plasma citrate levels, we propose a stepwise approach incorporating routinely measured screening tools and confirmatory parameters. Studies incorporating direct plasma citrate concentration measurements should be conducted to validate these criteria alongside readily available bedside surrogate markers. Refining this framework is essential to enhance the safe implementation of RCA and ultimately improve outcomes in critically ill patients.

item.category: Academic emergency medicine : official journal of the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine
item.description:
Background: Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (CHS) is an increasingly frequent emergency department (ED) presentation. Although ondansetron is commonly used, emerging evidence suggests haloperidol and droperidol may provide more effective symptom control. Robust comparative effectiveness data, particularly regarding short-term ED recidivism, remain limited.

Methods: We conducted a multicenter retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX Research Network from 2014 to 2024. Adults presenting to the ED with vomiting-related and cannabis-related ICD-10 diagnoses who received haloperidol, droperidol, or ondansetron during the index encounter were included. Patients with alternative causes of vomiting or major confounding conditions were excluded. Propensity-score matching was performed for three pairwise comparisons: haloperidol versus ondansetron, droperidol versus ondansetron, and droperidol versus haloperidol. The primary outcome was 72-h ED recidivism. Secondary outcomes included 72-h hospital admission, 7-day ED recidivism, and coded adverse events. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards modeling evaluated independent predictors of 72-h ED recidivism.

Results: After matching, haloperidol was associated with lower 72-h ED recidivism compared with ondansetron (8.2% vs. 15.1%; OR 0.50, 95% CI 0.41-0.62; p < 0.0001). Droperidol was also associated with lower 72-h ED recidivism compared with ondansetron (7.4% vs. 14.0%; OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.32-0.76; p = 0.0014). Droperidol and haloperidol did not differ significantly in 72-h ED recidivism (7.5% vs. 9.8%; OR 0.75, 95% CI 0.47-1.20; p = 0.23). In the multivariable model, haloperidol (HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.49-0.79) and droperidol (HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.56-0.83) were independently associated with lower return risk, whereas ondansetron was not. Coded adverse events were rare across all groups.

Conclusions: In this large multicenter cohort, haloperidol and droperidol were associated with lower short-term ED recidivism than ondansetron among adults meeting a suspected CHS phenotype. These findings support prospective studies evaluating haloperidol and droperidol for ED management of CHS, including optimal dosing, route, medication sequencing, discharge treatment, and safety monitoring.

item.title: Chest: Giving or Taking? Ethical Guidance for Hospital Administrators Involved in Organ Procurement
item.description:
Organ procurement from unrepresented decedents is legal in the United States, and some states even designate "the hospital administrator" as having the right to authorize donation. However, there is little guidance for an administrator to consult in their effort to make a socially responsible decision. In this case study, we review the arguments in favor of deferring, deciding against, or deciding in favor of authorization. We contend that that there are three reasons involving uncertainty, inequity, and the risk of mistrust that should give an administrator pause in endorsing organ procurement. We ultimately recommend that organ recovery should not be authorized unless there is (1) strong evidence that a diligent search for surrogates has been undertaken, establishing a reasonable amount of certainty that none are forthcoming, and (2) some evidence suggesting that the decedent would favor organ donation.

item.title: Chest: "Bold and necessary experiments:" The redelegation of authority and responsibility to nurses at the origins of cardiac intensive care
item.description:
Coronary Care Units (CCUs) were at the forefront of the development of intensive care in the 1960s and 1970s. The development of CCUs, and intensive care more broadly, was enabled by the interplay of expanding medical technology and the evolving role of nurses vis-à-vis physicians. This paper examines the history the CCU at New York Hospital, the teaching hospital of Cornell University School of Medicine and School of Nursing, with a particular focus on role of nurses in the unit's success. Drawing from historical archives of New York Hospital and the Cornell University School of Nursing, this paper argues that that nurses were co-creators, alongside physicians, of the NYH CCU, and demonstrates how nurses drew from the NYH CCU experience to expand critical care services at the local and national level, including by advocating for the creation of the NYH medical intensive care unit (MICU), leading a CCU nurse training program to expand regional CCU capability, and contributing expertise to a federally-sponsored national conference on CCUs. A close reading of this history offers lessons and insights as intensive care medicine moves into an uncertain future, chief among them that work of caring for critically ill patients requires the thoughtful integration of new technologies with hands on care.
