item.title: Lancet: Retinoblastoma
item.description:
Retinoblastoma, the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood, represents a substantial global health equity concern, exemplifying profound disparities in global burden and outcome despite being a largely curable cancer. Retinoblastoma is thought to arise from cone photoreceptor precursor cells of the developing retina, mainly driven by biallelic inactivation of the RB1 tumour suppressor gene. Fewer than 2% of cases have no detectable RB1 pathogenic variant; approximately half of these cases instead show high-level amplification of the MYCN oncogene. Diagnosis and monitoring currently rely on clinical examination and multimodal imaging. Emerging molecular diagnostic approaches such as aqueous humour liquid biopsy hold promise for minimally invasive tumour characterisation and real-time disease monitoring. Management has shifted towards eye-preserving strategies, with intra-arterial, intravitreal, and intracameral chemotherapy showing efficacy and safety. The global burden and mortality of retinoblastoma remains highest in regions with a low sociodemographic index, highlighting the need for continued interdisciplinary, equity-focused efforts to ensure timely diagnosis and accessible, high-quality care worldwide. This Seminar reviews the advances in retinoblastoma biology, diagnosis, treatment, survivorship, and global efforts to reduce inequities.

item.title: Lancet: Preparing for responsive management versus renal dialysis in older people living with kidney failure and frailty or multimorbidity in the UK (Prepare for Kidney Care): a two-arm, superiority, parallel-group, open-label, pragmatic, phase 3, individually randomised controlled trial
item.description:
Background: The comparative effectiveness of conservative kidney management and dialysis in older people (aged ≥80 years regardless of frailty and comorbidity or aged 65-79 years if frailty or multimorbidity are present) living with kidney failure is unknown. We aimed to assess the relative effectiveness of preparing for responsive management-a protocolised version of conservative kidney management-and preparing for renal dialysis.

Methods: Prepare for Kidney Care was a two-arm, superiority, parallel-group, open-label, pragmatic, phase 3, individually randomised controlled trial conducted in 31 kidney centres in England, Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland. Eligible patients had an estimated glomerular filtration rate below 15 mL/min per 1·73 m2, confirmed by at least one additional reading in the 12 months preceding consent that was not due to acute kidney injury, and were either aged 80 years or older, or aged 65-79 years with a WHO performance status of at least 3 or a Davies comorbidity score of at least 2. Eligible participants were randomly assigned (1:1) to prepare for responsive management-a patient-centred approach focused on slowing disease progression, active symptom management, and preserving quality of life without the use of dialysis or kidney transplantation-or to prepare for renal dialysis. Randomisation was stratified by centre and minimised by age; a centralised system ensured allocation concealment until randomisation had taken place. The primary outcome was the mean difference in quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs), combining length and health-related quality of life from the patient-reported EQ-5D-5L scale, including all follow-up from randomisation to Aug 31, 2025. The primary outcome was analysed by intention to treat in the full analysis set, which included all randomly assigned participants, with missing EQ-5D-5L values for living participants imputed. Harms (hospital admissions and dialysis access complications) and adverse events (deaths and hospital admissions, by cause) were assessed in the full analysis set. The trial was registered with ISRCTN, 17133653 (completed).

Findings: From July 1, 2017, to Aug 31, 2024, 6120 patients were screened across 31 kidney centres in the UK, 445 (7%) of whom were eligible and agreed to be randomly assigned. 228 (51%) of 445 participants were randomly assigned to prepare for responsive management and 217 (49%) of 445 participants were randomly assigned to prepare for renal dialysis. Median age was 82 years (IQR 80 to 86) and 137 (31%) of 445 participants were female. After a mean follow-up duration of 4·5 years (SD 2·1), mean QALYs were 1·354 (95% CI 1·201 to 1·508) in the prepare for responsive management group and 1·472 (1·288 to 1·655) in the prepare for renal dialysis group (adjusted mean difference -0·147 [95% CI -0·350 to 0·056] p=0·16). Specific harms outcomes were not prespecified, but hospital admission rates were similar in the two groups and dialysis access complications were significantly lower in the prepare for responsive management group (adjusted incident rate ratio 0·41 [95% CI 0·19 to 0·88]), based on 74 events in 36 participants across both groups. There were 667 serious adverse events in the prepare for responsive management group (157 [69%] of 228 participants died, with 510 hospital admissions) and 578 in the prepare for renal dialysis group (136 [63%] of 217 participants died, with 442 hospital admissions). None of these serious adverse events met the criteria for expedited reporting.

Interpretation: Among older people living with kidney failure and frailty or multimorbidity, we found no evidence that either preparing for responsive management or preparing for renal dialysis was superior in terms of QALYs over a mean follow-up duration of 4·5 years. This trial provides novel comparative information for clinical decision making.

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: A retrospective assessment of intubation prior to burn center arrival
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Pre-burn center intubation is frequently performed in burn patients with suspected inhalation injury because of concern for progressive airway edema. However, contemporary studies suggest that many of these intubations may be unnecessary. We evaluated factors associated with prolonged mechanical ventilation following pre-burn center intubation in burn-injured patients.

Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study of burn patients admitted to a single regional burn center from July 1, 2015, to June 30, 2023 who were intubated in the field or at referring facilities prior to arrival. Patients intubated through tracheostomy were excluded. Patients were stratified by duration of post-admission mechanical ventilation. Demographics, burn characteristics, inhalation injury findings, and documented intubation criteria were analyzed. Multivariate logistic regression identified factors associated with prolonged ventilation.

Results: Among 306 patients who met inclusion criteria, 147 (48%) were extubated within 24 h of admission. Patients requiring over 24 h of ventilation had larger burns, more inhalation injuries, longer hospital length of stay, and higher rates of ventilator-associated pneumonia and sepsis. Traditional findings such as singed facial hair, soot in the oropharynx, and suspected smoke inhalation poorly discriminated prolonged ventilator needs. Multivariate analysis demonstrated that indoor fire mechanism (OR 1.98, p = 0.004), signs of respiratory distress (OR 1.98, p = 0.008), and anticipated transfer of a patient with major burn without qualified medical professional to intubate en route (OR 2.69, p < 0.001) were associated with longer ventilation.

Conclusions: Our data suggests that physiology-based indicators of respiratory compromise may be more effective than traditional physical exam findings in optimizing airway management strategies before transfer to a burn center.

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: Layperson naloxone administration and subsequent emergency medical services care for opioid overdose
item.description:
Background: Layperson-administered naloxone is increasingly common before emergency medical services (EMS) arrival. However, EMS care following naloxone administered by laypeople rather than trained responders remains poorly characterized.

Methods: This cross-sectional study used the 2023 National EMS Information System dataset and included 9-1-1 activations for individuals aged ≥ 16 years with an EMS impression of opioid overdose and documented naloxone administration before EMS arrival. Exposures were layperson-administered naloxone (LAN) or trained responder-administered naloxone (TRAN; e.g., police, firefighter). The primary outcome was subsequent EMS naloxone administration. Secondary outcomes included total number of EMS naloxone administrations, advanced airway intervention, cardiac arrest, and EMS transport. We used descriptive statistics, t-tests, and multivariable logistic regression estimating adjusted odds ratios (aOR).

Results: Among 26,087 EMS activations, 8016 (30.7%) received LAN and 18,071 (69.3%) TRAN. Any subsequent EMS naloxone administration was less frequent following LAN (24.4% vs. 34.8%; P < .001); when EMS did administer additional naloxone, the mean number of administrations was slightly higher following LAN (mean difference 0.05, 95%CI 0.02-0.09; P = .001). Advanced airway attempts (1.6% vs. 1.4%, P = .160) and cardiac arrest (6.6% vs. 6.0%, P = .080) were uncommon. EMS transport occurred less often after LAN (79.4% vs. 84.4%, P < .001). In adjusted analyses, LAN was associated with lower odds of subsequent EMS naloxone administration (aOR 0.73; 95%CI 0.68-0.78) and EMS transport (aOR 0.78; 95%CI 0.73-0.84).

Conclusions: Layperson-administered naloxone was associated with less frequent EMS naloxone administration and lower rates of EMS transport. These findings support layperson overdose response while highlighting the need to better understand post-overdose care trajectories.

item.title: J Emerg Med: The Omokhodion Method: A High-Success, Low-Force Technique for Shoulder Dislocations
item.description:
Background: Shoulder dislocation is a common emergency presentation, and reduction may be complicated by pain, involuntary muscle guarding, patient positioning, clinician experience, associated injury, and the need for analgesia or procedural sedation. Because no single reduction maneuver is optimal for every patient or clinical setting, emergency physicians benefit from having multiple safe, reproducible, low-force techniques available.

Clinical problem: Many established reduction methods rely to varying degrees on traction, leverage, sustained positioning, or sequential rotation. Although these approaches may be effective, escalating force can worsen pain and protective muscular contraction in some patients, making reduction more difficult.

Technique: This technical report describes the Omokhodion method, a standardized low-force shoulder reduction technique based on upright positioning when feasible, continuous two-point support of the affected extremity, maintenance of approximately 90° of elbow flexion, supported abduction, controlled external rotation, gradual adduction toward the ipsilateral hip, and final internal rotation across the abdomen. Movement is performed slowly within the patient's tolerated range, and progression is paused when pain or guarding increases. Forceful longitudinal traction and abrupt leverage are avoided.

Discussion: The proposed biomechanical rationale is that continuous limb support, controlled positioning, progressive soft-tissue accommodation, and deliberate pacing may reduce gravitational loading and counterproductive muscle guarding while facilitating restoration of glenohumeral alignment. The method is intended to complement, not replace, established shoulder reduction techniques, and standard principles of neurovascular assessment, analgesia, procedural sedation, imaging, immobilization, and orthopedic consultation remain applicable.

Conclusion: The Omokhodion method provides a structured and reproducible low-force option for shoulder dislocation reduction and procedural education. Prospective clinical and biomechanical studies are needed to define its effectiveness, safety, optimal indications, reproducibility, and comparative performance relative to established reduction techniques.

item.title: J Emerg Med: Changes in Antiviral Treatment for Hospitalized Adults with Influenza in United States Emergency Departments
item.description:
Background: Early administration of an antiviral reduces influenza-related complications, and multiple guidelines recommend prompt antiviral treatment for all hospitalized patients with influenza. However, there is limited data on early antiviral treatment within the Emergency Department (ED).

Study objectives: Our epidemiological study assesses temporal trends in the initiation of antiviral treatment for adults hospitalized with influenza in the ED and identifies factors associated with nonadherence.

Methods: This retrospective cohort study examined antiviral treatment patterns among adults hospitalized with influenza in a U.S. ED from 2016 to 2025, using Epic Cosmos. Patients with ICD-10-coded or laboratory-confirmed influenza A/B were included. The primary outcome was the proportion of hospitalized patients who received oseltamivir, peramivir, baloxavir, or zanamivir in the ED.

Results: Of the 483,459 hospitalized ED patients with influenza, 416,982 (86.25%) received an antiviral in the ED. Antiviral treatment ranged from 72.7% in 2021 to 91.08% in 2020, rebounding to 85.11% in 2025. Differences in demographics between treated and untreated patients were observed across age, ethnicity, race, and spoken language. The likelihood of antiviral therapy was lower in the South (odds ratios [OR] 0.95; 95% confidence intervals [CI] 0.93-0.97) and West (OR 0.78; 95% CI 0.76-0.80) compared to the Northeast of the United States. The rate of antiviral treatment was moderately correlated with the national rate of influenza positivity in the ED (Pearson correlation 0.59).

Conclusion: Although prompt administration of an antiviral for hospitalized patients reduces influenza-related complications, antiviral administration is not universal in the ED. Our study highlights a critical gap that requires urgent implementation of mitigation strategies.

item.title: N Engl J Med: Plozasiran for Severe Hypertriglyceridemia and Risk of Pancreatitis
item.category: The New England journal of medicine
item.description:
Background: Severe hypertriglyceridemia is associated with an increased risk of acute pancreatitis. Plozasiran, a small interfering RNA targeting APOC3 messenger RNA, lowers triglyceride levels and potentially mitigates the risk of acute pancreatitis.

Methods: In two double-blind, placebo-controlled trials, 757 adults with severe hypertriglyceridemia were randomly assigned in a 2:1 ratio to receive plozasiran (25 mg) or placebo at baseline and at months 3, 6, and 9. These trials had identical designs, end points, and analytic plans. The primary end point was the percent change in the fasting plasma triglyceride level from baseline to month 12. Key secondary end points were the percent change in the fasting triglyceride level from baseline to month 10, a fasting triglyceride level of less than 500 mg per deciliter (5.6 mmol per liter) and less than 150 mg per deciliter (1.7 mmol per liter), the percent change in the fasting serum triglyceride level at month 12 for patients with a baseline triglyceride level of 880 mg per deciliter or greater, and changes in remnant cholesterol and non-HDL cholesterol. A pooled analysis addressed adjudicated acute pancreatitis, incidence, and first-event timing.

Results: At month 12, patients in the plozasiran groups had a median triglyceride level that was lower than the baseline level by 79% and 81% in the two trials. These reductions corresponded to a median difference in the plozasiran groups as compared with the placebo groups (placebo-adjusted change) of -45 percentage points (95% confidence interval [CI], -51 to -38) and -47 percentage points (95% CI, -54 to -39). A triglyceride level of less than 500 mg per deciliter at 12 months was reported in 91% and 93% of the patients in the plozasiran groups and in 51% and 50% of those in the placebo groups (P<0.001). The rates of acute pancreatitis were 1 per 100 patient-years with plozasiran and 5 per 100 patient-years with placebo (rate ratio, 0.22; P = 0.008). Adverse events during treatment occurred in 73% of the patients in both the pooled plozasiran and placebo groups.

Conclusions: Among patients with severe hypertriglyceridemia, the use of plozasiran resulted in lower triglyceride levels and a lower risk of acute pancreatitis than placebo at 12 months. item.title: Am J Respir Crit Care Med: Reduced desaturation-based detection of sleep apnea events in self-identified Black individuals across two cohorts
item.category: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
item.description:
Rationale: Pulse oximetry may overestimate oxygen saturation in individuals with darker skin pigmentation, potentially reducing detection of desaturation during sleep-disordered breathing.

Objectives: To assess racial/ethnic differences in desaturation-based obstructive event detection and cardiovascular risk, and evaluate heart-rate response as an oximetry-independent marker for risk stratification.

Methods: We analyzed participants without cardiovascular disease in the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis(MESA) and Sleep Heart Health Study(SHHS). We modeled desaturation-based AHI relative to airflow-defined AHI and examined AHI-ΔHR6, defined by respiratory events with a heart-rate increase ≥6 beats/min. Adjusted Cox models evaluated associations with a composite outcome, major adverse cardiovascular events or all-cause mortality(MACE/mortality).

Measurements and main results: Black participants had 21% and 20% lower proportions of airflow-defined events meeting the ≥4% desaturation criterion than White participants in MESA (ratio 0.79[95% CI,0.68-0.93]; p = 0.003) and SHHS (0.80[0.68-0.94]; p = 0.008), respectively. No other racial/ethnic group showed a lower proportion of airflow-defined events meeting desaturation criteria than White participants. AHI-ΔHR6 event detection was similar between Black and White participants in both cohorts. In Whites participants, desaturation-based events were associated with MACE/mortality in MESA but not in SHHS, while desaturation-based AHI measures were not significantly associated with MACE/mortality in Black individuals in either cohort. In contrast, AHI-ΔHR6 was associated with MACE/mortality in MESA (HR 1.33[1.09-1.63];p=0.006) and SHHS (1.26[1.02-1.55]; p = 0.033).

Conclusions: Desaturation-based scoring identified a lower proportion of reduced flow events in Black than White participants, whereas heart-rate-response-based event detection was similar across groups, suggesting oximetry-related under-detection in individuals with darker pigment.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: RELAX Perinatal Digital Intervention to Prevent Increasing Anxiety: A Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Anxiety disorders affect 1 in 5 pregnant women and birthing people. Cognitive bias modification for interpretation reduces anxiety and repetitive negative thinking (RNT; a risk factor for anxiety) among nonpregnant samples.

Objective: To evaluate whether adding pregnancy-tailored cognitive bias modification for interpretation to usual maternity care (UC) prevents increased anxiety during pregnancy; reduces anxiety, depression, and RNT before and after birth; and improves functioning before and after birth compared with UC.

Design, setting, and participants: The RELAX (Reducing Levels of Anxiety) 2-arm, parallel-group, multisite, superiority, phase 2b randomized clinical trial recruited participants from June 2023 to July 2024, with final assessment in April 2025. Participants included pregnant individuals in the UK at 16 to 28 weeks' gestation, with high RNT and up to moderate anxiety, recruited via antenatal clinics or self-referral.

Intervention: Participants were randomized to the self-led digital intervention (RELAX plus UC), involving twelve 17-minute sessions over 4 weeks, or to UC.

Main outcomes and measures: Assessments took place at baseline before randomization (T0) and 4 weeks (T1), 8 weeks (T2), and 36 weeks (T3; 12-24 weeks after birth) after randomization. The primary outcome was anxiety, as assessed by the 7-item Generalized Anxiety Disorder scale (GAD-7) at T2 and as a secondary outcome at T3. Secondary outcomes included RNT (assessed by the 10-item trait version of the Repetitive Thinking Questionnaire [RTQ-10]), depression (general and perinatal, assessed by the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 [PHQ-9] and Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale [EPDS]), perinatal anxiety (assessed by the Perinatal Anxiety Screening Scale [PASS]), worry (assessed by the Penn State Worry Questionnaire [PSWQ]), and functioning (assessed by the Work and Social Adjustment Scale [WSAS]). Interpretation bias at T1 was the hypothesized mechanism. Analysis was performed using a modified intention-to-treat approach.

Results: A total of 268 participants were randomized (mean [SD] age 33.7 [3.9] years; 174 [64.9%] married). Anxiety was significantly lower for RELAX participants vs UC (mean GAD-7 difference, -1.5; 95% CI, -2.4 to -0.6; P = .001). Depression (mean PHQ-9 difference, -0.8; 95% CI -1.5 to -0.1; and mean EPDS difference, -1.1; 95% CI, -2.0 to -0.2), RNT (mean RTQ-10 difference, -2.7; 95% CI, -4.5 to -0.9), worry (mean PSWQ difference, -3.6; 95% CI, -5.9 to -1.3), and perinatal anxiety (mean PASS difference, -5.5; 95% CI, -8.2 to -2.8) were significantly lower at T2. Effects on general anxiety (mean GAD-7 difference, -1.0; 95% CI, -1.9 to -0.1), postnatal depression (mean EPDS difference, -1.3; 95% CI, -2.4 to -0.2), and RNT (mean RTQ-10 difference, -2.4; 95% CI, -4.6 to -0.2) were sustained at T3. RELAX promoted more positive interpretations vs UC (mean difference, 2.1; 95% CI, 1.8-2.3) that did not mediate effects at T2 (indirect effect on GAD-7, -0.2; percentile bootstrap 95% CI, -0.4 to 0.1). Functioning did not differ at T2 (mean WSAS difference, -1.0; 95% CI, -2.5 to 0.5) or T3 (mean WSAS difference, -0.8; 95% CI, -2.7 to 1.2), nor did perinatal anxiety (mean PASS difference, -2.1; 95% CI, -5.5 to 1.4), general depression (mean PHQ-9 difference, -0.2; 95% CI, -1.2 to 0.9), or worry (mean PSWQ difference, -1.4; 95% CI, -4.1 to 1.3) at T3.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Gestational Age- and Altitude-Specific Hemoglobin Thresholds and Candidate Windows for Preterm Birth
item.description:
Importance: Maternal hemoglobin is a clinically accessible biomarker of preterm birth (PTB) risk, but abnormal thresholds are inconsistent and do not account for variation by gestational age or altitude.

Objectives: To evaluate the association between maternal hemoglobin concentration and PTB across gestational ages and altitudes, including PTB subtype, and to define gestational age-specific, altitude-adapted hemoglobin thresholds and assessment windows.

Design, setting, and participants: This multicenter, retrospective cohort study used a multisource database integrating electronic medical records, preconception examination, and geospatial data from 5 medical centers in Yunnan, China, a region with a marked altitudinal gradient, and consecutively included singleton pregnancies delivered between January 1, 2017, and July 31, 2025.

Exposure: Prepregnancy and prenatal hemoglobin values were assessed. Prenatal measurements were grouped into 2-week intervals (target gestational week ±7 days), with 36 weeks analyzed separately.

Main outcomes and measures: Preterm birth was operationally defined as live birth from 28 weeks 0 days through 36 weeks 6 days of gestation.

Results: Of 141 943 singleton live births among women (mean [SD] maternal age, 29.7 [4.6] years), 12 607 (8.88%) were PTBs. Maternal hemoglobin measurement showed a gestational age-dependent U-shaped association with PTB, and thresholds varied across gestation. Compared with the intermediate group, a low hemoglobin concentration measured at 13 weeks (<12.00 g/dL; adjusted odds ratio [AOR], 1.46; 95% CI, 1.17-1.80) was associated with PTB, persisting from 27 weeks onward (<11.00 g/dL; AOR, 1.48; 95% CI, 1.25-1.74). A high hemoglobin concentration from 19 weeks onward was associated with PTB (>13.50 g/dL; AOR, 1.28; 95% CI, 1.04-1.55). At high altitude, thresholds were generally higher, and a low hemoglobin concentration from 21 weeks was persistently associated with PTB. Subtype analyses showed earlier low hemoglobin concentration associations for medically indicated PTB and middle- to late-pregnancy high hemoglobin concentration associations for both subtypes.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study, hemoglobin thresholds associated with PTB varied across gestation and were generally higher at high altitude; low- and high-hemoglobin assessment windows differed and varied by altitude. These findings may help refine gestational age- and altitude-specific interpretation of routine hemoglobin measurements and PTB risk assessment, pending external validation.

item.description:
Importance: Midostaurin and quizartinib are approved with intensive chemotherapy (IC) in patients with newly diagnosed FLT3 internal tandem duplication (ITD)-positive acute myeloid leukemia (AML), but no randomized clinical trials have directly compared them.

Objective: To compare 1-year overall survival (OS) among patients with FLT3-ITD variant AML initiating IC with midostaurin or quizartinib.

Design, setting, and participants: This multicenter, retrospective cohort study included patients with newly diagnosed FLT3-ITD variant AML treated at 12 US referral centers between January 1, 2018, and May 31, 2025. Data analysis was performed from January 2026 to August 2026.

Exposures: Induction therapy with IC plus midostaurin or quizartinib.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was 1-year overall survival (OS). Secondary outcomes included 1-year event-free survival (EFS), induction response, and hematopoietic cell transplant (HCT) rates at first remission; FLT3 clearance after induction was exploratory. Safety outcomes included rates of febrile neutropenia, infections, intensive care unit use, total parenteral nutrition and granulocyte colony-stimulating factor use, discharge to a rehabilitation facility after index hospitalization, and early mortality. Cox proportional hazards regression models were adjusted for baseline covariates and HCT as time dependent.

Results: Among 215 patients (median [IQR] age, 56.0 [45.0-65.0] years; 119 [55.3%] female), 127 (59.1%) received midostaurin and 88 (40.9%) received quizartinib. Median (IQR) follow-up was 667.0 (289.0-1368.0) days for midostaurin and 324.0 (168.0-546.5) days for quizartinib, reflecting the latter's more recent approval. One-year OS was 78.0% for midostaurin and 93.0% for quizartinib (hazard ratio [HR], 0.22; 95% CI, 0.08-0.58; P = .002). The 1-year EFS was 56.0% for midostaurin and 77.0% for quizartinib (HR, 0.43; 95% CI, 0.25-0.74; P = .003). Patients receiving quizartinib had higher rates of composite complete remission (75 [85.2%] vs 93 [73.2%]; P = .03), whereas rates of FLT3 clearance after induction (20 [38.5%] for quizartinib vs 27 [40.3%] for midostaurin; P = .84) and HCT in first remission (47 [53.4%] for quizartinib vs 83 [65.4%] for midostaurin; P = .08) were comparable. A sensitivity analysis limited to patients treated in 2023 or later (more balanced follow-up) showed directionally consistent but nonsignificant OS and EFS differences.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of adults with FLT3-ITD variant AML, IC plus quizartinib was associated with improved 1-year survival, induction response, and safety compared with IC plus midostaurin.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Body Mass Index, Genetic Predisposition, and Obesity-Related Second Cancer Risk in Cancer Survivors
item.description:
Importance: Excess body weight is an established risk factor for second primary cancers (SPCs) among cancer survivors. Whether genetic susceptibility to higher body mass index (BMI) is associated with the risk of obesity-related SPCs remains unclear.

Objective: To examine associations of genetic predisposition to higher BMI with the risk of obesity-related SPCs and its joint association with BMI.

Design, setting, and participants: This prospective cohort study used data from the Cancer Prevention Study II Nutrition Cohort, a large prospective study of adults residing in 21 states in the US who were cancer-free at the time of the 1992 survey and responded to biennial follow-up questionnaires starting in 1997. Response rates to the biennial questionnaires ranged from 78.1% to 92.1%. Participants for this analysis included cancer survivors who received a diagnosis of a first primary, nonmetastatic invasive cancer between 1992 and 2015, provided a biospecimen sample, and were followed up through 2017. Analyses were conducted between September 2025 and August 2026.

Exposures: A polygenic score for BMI (PGS-BMI) and BMI.

Main outcomes and measures: Cox proportional hazards models were used to evaluate associations between PGS-BMI and obesity-related SPC risk, as well as between BMI and obesity-related SPC risk stratified by PGS-BMI tertiles.

Results: This analysis included 14 309 cancer survivors. Their median (IQR) age at first cancer diagnosis was 72.9 (68.2-77.4) years. Approximately 58.6% (8378) of survivors were male, and 58.6% (8382) had a BMI in the overweight (25 to <30) or obese (≥30) range. During a median (IQR) follow-up of 9.1 (4.6-14.2) years, there were 722 (5.0%) obesity-related SPCs. Compared with survivors in the lowest PGS-BMI tertile, those in the highest tertile had greater risk of obesity-related SPCs (hazard ratio [HR], 1.26 [95% CI, 1.06-1.51]). Obesity was associated with increased risk across tertiles of the PGS-BMI without evidence of interaction (P = .89 for interaction). Compared with survivors with low genetic predisposition and BMI lower than 25, those with low genetic predisposition and obesity had higher obesity-related SPC risk (HR, 1.59 [95% CI, 1.21-2.09]) and those with high genetic predisposition and obesity had the highest risk (HR, 1.82 [95% CI, 1.38-2.40]). The 10-year cumulative incidence ranged from 3.4% (95% CI, 2.9%-4.0%) to 5.1% (95% CI, 4.3%-5.9%) across joint exposure groups.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of cancer survivors, genetic susceptibility to higher BMI was associated with a modestly increased risk of obesity-related SPCs, whereas obesity was associated with greater risk regardless of genetic predisposition. These findings underscore the importance of weight management for all cancer survivors and suggest that a meaningful proportion of obesity-related SPCs may be preventable.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: External Validation of a Machine Learning Model for Delirium Risk
item.description:
Importance: Although external validation of machine learning (ML)-based delirium risk models is a key stage in the model development pipeline, few published reports exist. Moreover, ML-based delirium risk models commonly degrade in performance during external validation.

Objective: To examine the performance of a fusion multimodal with natural language processing (NLP) delirium risk stratification model in live clinical practice with cross-hospital external validation.

Design, setting, and participants: This quality improvement study evaluated live clinical deployment of the model among patients 60 years or older who were admitted to non-intensive care units at Mount Sinai Hospital (MSH), with external validation performed at Mount Sinai Morningside Hospital (MSM), from December 1, 2024, to December 31, 2025.

Main outcomes and measures: Primary outcomes were performance of the risk stratification model, assessed by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), and monthly delirium detection rates. A 2 × 2 confusion matrix was created, and the 4 cells were used to calculate model performance metrics and compare associated diagnostic yield between premodel deployment and active model deployment periods.

Results: The overall sample included 33 095 admissions to non-intensive care units at MSM and MSH (mean [SD] age, 74.86 (9.22) years; 15 601 women [47.1%], 17 271 men [52.2%]). A total of 9020 MSM inpatient admissions were assigned a delirium risk score by the risk stratification model during live clinical operations and were compared to 21 186 MSH inpatient admissions that were assigned a risk score by the same model. Age at admission significantly differed between patients at MSM and MSH (MSM: median [IQR] age, 75.79 [68.25-83.88] years vs MSH: 72.62 [66.64-79.65] years; P < .001). Patients from MSM and MSH also significantly differed by sex, race and ethnicity, surgical vs medical primary diagnosis, length of stay, and dementia prevalence rate. Among 11 909 MSM patients, patients in the pre-ML cohort (median [IQR] age, 78.00 [71.00-85.00] years) were significantly older than those in the post-ML cohort (median [IQR] age, 75.79 [68.25-83.88] years) (P < .001). The AUROC of the model was 0.91 (95% CI, 0.90-0.92) for MSM and 0.94 (95% CI, 0.93-0.94) for MSH. The positive predictive value of the model was 25.9% for MSM and 19.4% for MSH. For MSM, the mean monthly delirium detection rate significantly increased from 9.23% (95% CI, 8.07%-10.38%) to 19.59% (95% CI, 17.32%-21.85%) after model deployment (P < .001).

Conclusions and relevance: In this quality improvement study, an ML-based delirium risk stratification model maintained acceptable discriminative performance during external deployment without retraining and was similar to its performance at the development site without retraining. Model deployment was also associated with increased diagnostic yield but a high false positive rate. These findings provide further evidence of the potential generalizability of the model.

item.title: JAMA Intern Med: Risk of Shoulder Injury Related to Vaccine Administration for COVID-19 and Influenza Vaccinations
item.description:
Importance: The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine identified a critical evidence gap regarding the risk of shoulder injury related to vaccine administration (SIRVA) after COVID-19 vaccination.

Objective: To compare the risk of SIRVA after COVID-19 vs influenza vaccinations in adults.

Design, setting, and participants: This population-based cohort study included individuals aged at least 18 years who received a COVID-19 or influenza vaccination administered via intramuscular deltoid injection between August 1, 2023, and April 30, 2024, at Kaiser Permanente Southern California. Data were analyzed from June 2024 to September 2026.

Exposure: Receipt of COVID-19 vaccination or influenza vaccination.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was incident SIRVA, defined as shoulder symptoms beginning at or before 7 days and persisting more than 30 days after vaccination, identified using a validated natural language processing algorithm. Incidences were calculated per 10 000 vaccinations. Adjusted relative risks (RRs), risk differences, and 95% CIs were estimated using robust Poisson regression with inverse probability of treatment weighting.

Results: A total of 1 366 362 individuals (mean [SD] age at vaccination, 58.4 [18.2] years; 782 994 female [57.3%]) across 1 901 588 vaccinations were included (1 076 609 vaccinations [56.7%] were administered to females). Among 1 830 636 vaccinations in the primary analysis, 252 SIRVA cases were identified as follows: 110 cases (0.018%) after 596 614 COVID-19 vaccinations and 142 cases (0.012%) after 1 234 022 influenza vaccinations. An additional 13 SIRVA cases (0.018%) were identified among 70 952 simultaneous COVID-19 and influenza vaccinations. Most COVID-19 vaccines were Pfizer-BioNTech messenger RNA (667 455 of 667 566 [99.98%]), and influenza vaccines were predominantly standard-dose (866 530 of 1 304 974 [66.40%]) or high-dose (438 183 of 1 304 974 [33.58%]) inactivated quadrivalent formulations. SIRVA incidence was higher after COVID-19 than influenza vaccination, at an incidence of 1.84 (95% CI, 1.53-2.22) vs 1.15 (95% CI, 0.98-1.36) per 10 000 vaccinations, corresponding to an adjusted absolute increase of 0.67 cases (95% CI, 0.15-1.19) per 10 000 vaccinations (adjusted RR, 1.63; 95% CI, 1.16-2.28). Among adults 65 years or older, SIRVA incidence was 2.11 (95% CI, 1.67-2.67) per 10 000 for COVID-19 vaccination and 1.63 (95% CI, 1.28-2.07) per 10 000 for high-dose influenza vaccination (adjusted RR, 1.41; 95% CI, 0.92-2.15).

Conclusions and relevance: Results of this cohort study suggest that although SIRVA was rarely associated with both vaccines, COVID-19 vaccination was associated with approximately 7 additional cases per 100 000 vaccinations compared with influenza vaccination. Among adults aged 65 years or older, SIRVA risk did not differ significantly between COVID-19 and high-dose influenza vaccination. The small absolute risk of SIRVA should be considered alongside the established benefits of COVID-19 and influenza vaccination in preventing severe disease and hospitalization.

item.title: Lancet: Long-term outcomes after percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stents versus coronary artery bypass grafting for left main coronary artery disease: a prospective analysis of the multicentre IRIS-MAIN registry
item.description:
Background: Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with drug-eluting stents has been widely used to treat patients with left main coronary artery disease; however, long-term comparative outcomes versus coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) in real-world populations remain poorly characterised. We aimed to compare long-term all-cause mortality after PCI or CABG in Asian patients with unprotected left main coronary artery disease.

Methods: We analysed prospectively collected data from the multicentre IRIS-MAIN registry, conducted at 46 hospitals in South Korea, India, Japan, Indonesia, and Malaysia. The registry enrolled adults aged 18 years or older with unprotected left main coronary artery disease (defined as a stenosis diameter of ≥50% as visually estimated on angiography), who had been treated with PCI, CABG, or medical therapy alone. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality. We used a target trial emulation framework to compare the long-term risk of all-cause mortality between PCI with drug-eluting stents and isolated CABG. We used propensity-score overlap weighting to adjust for measured baseline covariates. The IRIS-MAIN Registry study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT01341327).

Findings: Between Jan 1, 2003, and Dec 31, 2024, 6900 patients were enrolled in the IRIS-MAIN registry, of whom 5379 (78·0%) underwent coronary revascularisation through either PCI with drug-eluting stents (3836 [71·3%]) or CABG (1543 [28·7%]) and were included in the analysis. The median duration of follow-up for all patients was 10·0 years (IQR 5·0-16·7). In the overlap-weighted population, no statistically detectable difference in 10-year weighted Kaplan-Meier rates of all-cause mortality was observed between PCI and CABG (24·0% vs 22·9%; overlap-weighted hazard ratio 1·00 [95% CI 0·87-1·14]; p=0·99). The confidence interval does not exclude a mortality benefit or harm with either strategy.

Interpretation: In this non-randomised registry analysis of patients with left main coronary artery disease, there was no statistically detectable difference in all-cause mortality between PCI and CABG. For patients considered suitable for either strategy, multidisciplinary Heart Team discussion might help patients and clinicians weigh potential trade-offs in the choice between PCI and CABG. These findings are observational and cannot establish causal treatment effects or equivalence in survival.

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Ultrasound-guided hydrodissection for anterior cutaneous nerve entrapment syndrome: A case series
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Anterior cutaneous nerve entrapment syndrome (ACNES) is an uncommon, non-emergent cause of chronic abdominal wall pain arising from entrapment of the terminal branches of the T7-T12 intercostal nerves at the anterior rectus sheath. It is usually recognized only after laboratory and imaging studies have excluded intra-abdominal causes, often after repeated evaluations. Prior abdominal surgery is a recognized risk factor due to fascial scarring. Ultrasound-guided hydrodissection with 5% dextrose in water (D5W) and dilute lidocaine has been described in case reports as a minimally invasive treatment that may relieve pain and release the entrapped nerve. We present two patients who developed post-surgical ACNES following laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and laparoscopic cholecystectomy, respectively. Each presented to the ED with severe abdominal wall pain (NRS 9/10 and 10/10) and negative intra-abdominal workup. Both patients met diagnostic criteria including positive Carnett's sign, positive pinch test, and >90% pain reduction after ultrasound-guided hydrodissection. On chart review, pain relief was sustained at 6 weeks (Case 1) and 4 weeks (Case 2), and neither patient received other treatment after discharge. In these selected patients, bedside ultrasound-guided hydrodissection was feasible and was followed by rapid pain relief. Prospective, comparative studies are needed to establish its place within the ACNES treatment algorithm and to assess durability beyond the short-term follow-up reported here.

Background: Closed-loop communication of critical and urgent imaging findings is essential for patient safety, but traditional verbal-only workflows can introduce friction and limit communication throughput. Epic Secure Chat, an EHR-integrated messaging platform, may reduce friction while preserving closed-loop communication requirements. This study evaluated communication volume, radiologist interpretation throughput, clinician experience, and reported safety events following implementation of a Secure Chat-first protocol.

Methods: A prospective pre-post cohort study of operational outcomes was conducted across 26 emergency departments within a large academic health system, with a concurrent post-implementation survey. Following a 205-day overnight Secure Chat pilot, operational data were compared with a 161-day pre-implementation period using paired t-tests. Communication and examination volumes were normalized by time period. Linear regression was used to assess the association between Secure Chat volume and interpretation throughput change.

Results: Survey responses were obtained from 48 emergency physicians (20.2%) and 19 radiologists (48.7%). No Secure Chat-associated safety events were identified across 1087 reviewed communications.

Conclusion: Implementation of a Secure Chat-first protocol with a verbal failsafe was associated with increased communication volume without a reduction in radiologist throughput or identified safety events.

item.title: Prehosp Emerg Care: Transcutaneous Pacing in the Prehospital Setting - A Retrospective Cohort Study of Electrical Capture
item.description:
Objectives: Transcutaneous pacing (TCP) treats hemodynamically unstable bradycardia refractory to pharmacologic management. Effective TCP requires electrical and mechanical capture to augment perfusion. Little is known about prehospital TCP and capture incidence.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients treated with prehospital TCP by an emergency medical services agency between 2017 and 2024. Continuous ECG recordings from cardiac monitors were reviewed. Electrical capture was the primary outcome, defined as a widened QRS with a distinct T wave following a TCP spike. Secondary measures included capture duration, clinician-verbalized pulse during pacing, plethysmograph waveform alignment, and changes in systolic blood pressure (SBP), pulse oximetry, and end-tidal carbon dioxide.

Results: Fifty-six patients received attempted TCP. Median age was 70 years (interquartile range [IQR] 58-85), and 34% were female. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) was administered in 59% of patients. Electrical capture was achieved in 18 patients (32%). Among patients who achieved electrical capture, complete capture occurred a mean of 27.2% (standard deviation 30.5%) of attempted pacing duration. The median SBP change was +22.0 (IQR: -2-82) mmHg in patients with electrical capture and 0.0 (IQR: -29-7) mmHg in those with only rare-to-absent capture (p = 0.031). During TCP, clinicians verbalized a palpable pulse 26 times across 19 patients. Only 4 instances (15%) coincided with electrical capture.

Conclusions: Electrical capture during prehospital TCP occurred in a minority of patients and was often intermittent. Prehospital identification of mechanical capture using routine clinical indicators was difficult and unreliable. Future work should standardize capture definitions and physiologic measurements to determine when TCP produces clinically meaningful perfusion.

item.title: Prehosp Emerg Care: The Accuracy and Precision of Gravity-Driven Infusions
item.description:
Objectives: When infusion pumps are unavailable in the prehospital setting, clinicians must estimate fluid flow by counting drops in a drip chamber. We aimed to assess the accuracy and precision of gravity-driven infusions and to estimate the magnitude of inaccuracy and imprecision attributable to human and non-human factors.

Methods: We recruited 55 paramedics to participate in structured, experimental, simulated study under controlled laboratory conditions, in which each participant set nine drip rates as accurately as possible on a standardized setup. Measurements of flow were made visually (drip rate) and volumetrically (delivered fluid). Volumetric measurements were used to represent overall error, visual measurements were used to represent human error, and the difference was used to represent non-human error. We measured accuracy (percentage error) and precision (mean absolute deviation) using the natural log of error factor to represent the multiplicative decomposition of human and non-human error additively. Mixed effect models were used to assess accuracy and precision across targeted drip rates.

Results: Inaccuracy and imprecision varied by targeted drip rate. Overall inaccuracy ranged from -45.3% (95%CI, -52.7% to -36.8%) to 5.8% (95%CI, -8.5% to 22.3%). Human inaccuracy ranged from -38.8% (95%CI, -46.0% to -30.8%) to 44.1% (95%CI, 27.1% to 63.4%). Non-human inaccuracy ranged from -26.7% (95%CI, -30.1% to -23.2%) to -6.8% (95%CI -11.1% to -2.3%). Imprecision was primarily driven by human factors. The degree of human variation between trial participants ranged from 24.2% (95%CI, 15.3% to 33.7%) to 43.7% (95%CI, 33.4% to 54.9%) across targeted rates. The targeted drip rate of 1gtt/s was more accurate than the pool of all other targeted rates (absolute error 31.1% versus 48.5%). Targeted drip rates of whole numbers were more accurate than targeted drip rates of fractional numbers (absolute error 40.7% versus 54.1%). Targeted drip rates below 1gtt/s were more accurate than rates above 1gtt/s (absolute error 35.3% versus 63.1%).

Conclusions: Gravity-driven fluid delivery exhibits inaccuracy and imprecision, which varies by targeted rate. While potentially modifiable human factors may improve the accuracy of this technique, non-human error contributes substantially to inaccuracy. There is a need to assess whether this inaccuracy and imprecision adversely affect patient outcomes.

item.title: J Addict Med: Medetomidine: Dose-Response Approach to Drug Monitoring
item.description:
Drug supply monitoring programs commonly describe novel substances in binary terms: a substance is either present or absent, and its presence alone defines risk. Medetomidine, a veterinary imidazole alpha-2 agonist anesthetic, has been detected as an adulterant in illegally manufactured fentanyl across the United States, and reports of medetomidine toxicity have been similarly widespread. Yet its severe withdrawal syndrome has emerged in communities more gradually, with many unaffected. The environmental-health concept of dose-response offers a plausible explanation for this geographic mismatch. Some harms follow a linear relationship where any exposure carries risk, and that risk rises in proportion to dose. Opioid overdose and medetomidine toxicity fit this pattern. Others may follow a threshold relationship, appearing only once exposure surpasses a critical level. Medetomidine withdrawal fits the threshold pattern because tolerance, and therefore withdrawal, require sustained exposure of sufficient dose and duration. Where it has appeared, the withdrawal syndrome has strained local hospital systems. Preliminary review of hospital billing data and community drug-checking results suggests that hospital utilization rose only after medetomidine's prevalence and potentially concentration in the local supply crossed a threshold. Current evidence supporting application of this dose-response theory to medetomidine withdrawal is hypothesis-generating. Further work linking drug-supply prevalence and concentration data to well-defined, drug-specific clinical outcomes could support a surveillance system that lets public health and hospital stakeholders anticipate drug-related harms before they become widespread, using evidence-based thresholds.

item.title: J Addict Med: How Should Stimulant Deaths Be Counted? A Cross-Sectional Analysis of Deaths Attributed to Opioids, Stimulants, or Alcohol
item.description:
Introduction: The different ways deaths are counted for surveillance-all attributable to alcohol versus acute toxicity for opioids or stimulants-have profound implications for understanding mortality and deploying prevention interventions.

Objectives: To explore alternative strategies to count stimulant (cocaine, psychostimulants) deaths.

Methods: We grouped substance-attributable deaths in San Francisco, CA, from 2015 to 2024 into mutually exclusive categories by involved substance (opioids, stimulants, alcohol). We used multivariable Poisson regression to determine prevalence ratios of additional contributing conditions (any, cardiac/hypertensive, or hepatobiliary and pancreatic) for each drug category, adjusted for age, sex, and race/ethnicity. We then used a postestimation technique to calculate adjusted predicted prevalence rates for each group.

Results: The adjusted prevalence ratio of any additional conditions was significantly different across substance-attributable death categories (P<0.001). Compared to stimulant deaths, opioid deaths had significantly lower prevalence of additional conditions [adjusted prevalence ratios (aPR): 0.51, 95% CI: 0.48-0.55], while alcohol deaths had higher prevalence (aPR: 1.24, 95% CI: 1.18-1.30). Opioid and alcohol deaths had a lower prevalence of cardiovascular conditions compared to stimulant deaths. Stimulant and alcohol deaths occurred at older ages than opioid deaths.

Conclusions: More stimulant- and alcohol-attributable deaths without opioids include complex medical conditions compared to opioid deaths. Counting all attributable stimulant deaths, excluding opioids, may improve our understanding of these deaths and interventions to address health consequences of stimulant use.

item.title: J Addict Med: Assessment of Health Care Worker Stigma Toward Pregnant People With Opioid Use Disorder
item.description:
Objectives: Stigma within health care can negatively affect pregnancy outcomes. Prior vignette studies suggest stigma varies by treatment status, but this has not been examined among pregnant people with opioid use disorder (OUD). We aimed to assess public stigma among health care workers toward pregnant people with OUD receiving medication for OUD (MOUD) versus actively using opioids and examine differences by clinical role and specialty.

Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional survey of staff (residents/fellows, clinicians, nurses, clinical support staff, ancillary staff, and medical students) solicited through email and public postings at a tertiary care hospital from May to November 2023. Eligible participants were 18 years or older and worked in roles interacting with pregnant patients. Participants were randomized to 1 of 2 vignettes describing a pregnant patient with OUD receiving methadone or actively using heroin. Stigma was assessed using a modified Attribution Questionnaire (mAQ-11), including parenting confidence and custody items. Differences across vignettes, clinical roles, and specialties were analyzed using ANOVA, with P<0.05 considered significant.

Results: Among 374 participants (MOUD n=183; heroin use n=191), stigma was significantly higher for active heroin use than the MOUD vignette (mean mAQ-11: 42.53 vs. 34.57, P<0.001). In the heroin-use vignette, clinicians endorsed less stigma than nurses and other medical professionals (P<0.001). Pediatric/neonatal clinicians endorsed greater stigma than obstetric clinicians (P=0.03). MOUD vignette participants expressed greater confidence in parenting ability and support for custody retention (P<0.001).

Conclusions: Health care worker stigma toward pregnant people with OUD was greatest in active opioid use vignettes. Differences across clinical roles and specialties identify important targets for antistigma interventions.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Managing Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth in Pediatric Short Bowel Syndrome: A Consensus Statement
item.description:
Importance: Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) is a common and clinically important complication of short bowel syndrome (SBS) in children, contributing to feeding intolerance, malabsorption, bloodstream infections, and frequent antibiotic exposure. Diagnostic and management practices vary widely across centers, and no rigorously developed, evidence-informed pediatric-specific guidance currently exists.

Objective: To develop international, pediatric-specific, expert consensus recommendations for the diagnosis and management of SIBO in children with SBS, with emphasis on diagnostic approach, antibiotic therapy, treatment response, and prevention.

Evidence review: A modified Delphi process was conducted between April 4, 2024, and February 18, 2025. A 7-member steering committee reviewed pediatric and adult SIBO literature using the terms small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth, short bowel syndrome, intestinal failure, and pediatric. Because pediatric-specific data were limited and study designs were heterogeneous, systematic reviews and meta-analyses were not feasible. Fifty-five international experts from multidisciplinary intestinal rehabilitation programs in North America and Europe were invited to participate in 3 rounds of anonymous online surveys and 2 in-person moderated consensus meetings. Draft statements were iteratively refined. Consensus was defined a priori as agreement of 75% or greater among respondents.

Findings: Completed surveys were received from 33 participants in round 1, 38 in round 2, and 28 in round 3. Consensus was achieved on 21 statements involving diagnostic approaches, therapeutic strategies, and monitoring practices. Recommendations addressed the use of breath testing and clinical criteria, indications for empiric antibiotic therapy and cycling, antibiotic selection and duration, and dietary considerations. Symptomatic improvement was considered an acceptable indicator of treatment response. Metronidazole was identified as the preferred first-line antibiotic, and long-term antibiotic cycling was supported for selected patients with recurrent, treatment-responsive SIBO. Collectively, the statements provide a practical framework to support consistent clinical decision-making in pediatric SBS-associated SIBO.

Conclusions and relevance: This Delphi-based consensus provides the first international pediatric-specific guidance for diagnosing and managing SIBO in children with SBS. Implementation of these recommendations may reduce practice variability, support more judicious antibiotic use, and improve patient outcomes while establishing a foundation for future research in this high-risk population.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Early Metformin Initiation and Glycemic Outcomes in Gestational Diabetes: A Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Conventional approaches to analyzing composite end points in clinical trials may not fully capture clinically meaningful treatment effects.

Objective: To estimate treatment effects of early metformin initiation on clinically ordered glycemic outcomes (insulin initiation and fasting hyperglycemia at gestational weeks 32 and 38) using generalized pairwise comparisons (GPCs).

Design, setting, and participants: This secondary analysis of a double-masked, placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial (conducted from June 2017 through September 2022) at 2 centers in Ireland (1 tertiary hospital and 1 regional hospital) included participants with gestational diabetes based on World Health Organization 2013 criteria. Participants were followed up through 12 weeks post partum. The data analysis was performed between October 18, 2025, and February 2, 2026.

Intervention: Participants were randomized 1:1 to metformin (maximum dose, 2500 mg) or matching placebo, in addition to usual care.

Main outcomes and measures: Generalized pairwise comparisons were performed using (1) a prioritized hierarchy (insulin initiation, fasting hyperglycemia at week 32, and fasting hyperglycemia at week 38) and (2) nonprioritized analyses of each end point, with overall summaries using equal weights and prespecified clinical weights (0.50, 0.25, and 0.25, respectively). Treatment effect sizes were summarized using win ratio (WR), net treatment benefit (NTB), and win odds (WO).

Results: Of 535 randomized pregnancies, 526 (262 placebo [49.0%] and 264 metformin [51.0%]; mean [SD] age of participants, 34.4 [4.8] years) had primary outcome data. Prioritized GPCs favored metformin over placebo for the composite outcome (WR, 1.46 [95% CI, 1.13-1.89]; NTB, 13.7 percentage points [95% CI, 4.3-22.8 percentage points]; WO, 1.34 [95% CI, 1.10-1.64]) (P = .004). The largest separation was observed for insulin initiation (WR, 1.68 [95% CI, 1.19-2.38]; NTB, 12.7 percentage points [95% CI, 4.2-21.0 percentage points]) (P = .003). Nonprioritized overall summaries favored metformin (WR, 1.53 [95% CI, 1.16-2.01]; NTB, 7.5 percentage points [95% CI, 2.7-12.3 percentage points]; WO, 1.32 [95% CI, 1.10-1.57]) (P = .002), with consistent clinically weighted results (WR, 1.57 [95% CI, 1.19-2.08]; NTB, 8.8 percentage points [95% CI, 3.4-14.2 percentage points]; WO, 1.39 [95% CI, 1.14-1.70]) (P = .001).

Conclusions and relevance: In this secondary analysis of a randomized clinical trial, prioritized and nonprioritized GPCs yielded statistically significant overall estimates favoring early metformin initiation over placebo across insulin initiation and fasting hyperglycemia outcomes. These findings complement the original primary analysis, provide a more clinically interpretable assessment of the composite outcome, and may inform prospective end point design in future trials.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Spousal Traumatic Brain Injury and Risk of Mortality, Dementia, and Cardiovascular Events
item.description:
Importance: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is highly prevalent in older adults. While there is strong and growing evidence that TBI is associated with caregiver burden and psychological health, it remains unclear whether a spouse's TBI is associated with the long-term health of the uninjured partner.

Objective: To evaluate whether having a spouse who sustains an incident TBI is associated with risk of mortality, dementia, and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and to assess whether associations differ by sex or survival of the injured spouse after TBI.

Design, setting, and participants: This prospective community-based cohort of married couples was performed at 4 US centers in North Carolina, Mississippi, Minnesota, and Maryland as part of the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) Study. Of 4506 baseline spousal pairs, 3281 were retained for mortality and dementia analyses and 2740 of these for MACE analyses. Participants contributed person-time from baseline (1987-1989) until incident outcome, death, loss to follow-up, divorce or separation, or administrative censoring on December 31, 2022. Analyses were conducted from November 24, 2025, through August 25, 2026.

Exposure: Incident spousal TBI (ascertained using self-report, hospitalization surveillance, and linked Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services data), modeled as a 2-category time-varying exposure (spousal TBI vs no spousal TBI) and 4-category exposure incorporating spousal death.

Main outcomes and measures: Incident all-cause mortality, dementia, and MACE. Cox proportional hazards regression shared frailty models were used to estimate associations adjusted for demographic, clinical, and behavioral characteristics.

Results: Among 3281 married pairs included in mortality and dementia analyses (among whom, 2740 pairs were included in MACE analyses), the mean (SD) age at baseline was 54.5 (5.5) years, with 3281 female and 3281 male spouses (for a total of 6562 participants). The median follow-up was 19.5 (IQR, 10.6-29.0) years. Spousal TBI was associated with increased risk of mortality (hazard ratio [HR], 1.24 [95% CI, 1.07-1.43]; P = .004) but not dementia (HR, 1.17 [95% CI, 0.88-1.56]; P = .28) or MACE (HR, 1.15 [95% CI, 0.84-1.57]; P = .40). In sex-stratified analyses, associations were similar among males and females. In models incorporating spousal death, mortality risk was higher among individuals whose spouse was alive with a TBI (HR, 1.22 [95% CI, 1.05-1.41]; P = .008), higher among those whose spouse was deceased without a TBI (HR, 1.48 [95% CI, 1.36-1.61]; P < .001), and higher among those whose spouse was deceased with a TBI (HR, 1.27 [95% CI, 1.07-1.52]; P = .006) compared with those whose spouse was alive without a TBI. Results were similar, but less precise, for dementia and MACE.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of married pairs of participants in the ARIC Study, having a spouse who sustained a TBI was associated with a modest but significantly higher risk of mortality in the uninjured partner, whereas findings for dementia and major adverse cardiovascular events were less consistent. These findings suggest that the consequences of TBI may extend beyond injured individuals and support family- and care partner-centered approaches to care.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Noninpatient Alternative Treatment Venues for Acute Care Needs
item.description:
Importance: Hospitalizations are costly and may lead to adverse events. Some health systems offer treatment in alternative venues of care for select patients.

Objective: To describe use and short-term outcomes of emergency department (ED) patients transitioned to noninpatient care settings (ambulatory treatment center [ATC], advanced care at home [ACAH], or emergency department observation unit [EDOU]) compared with inpatient care.

Design, setting, and participants: This retrospective cohort study of ED patients aged 19 years or older was conducted from January 1, 2024, to June 30, 2025, at multisite community ED and inpatient medical centers within an integrated delivery system (Kaiser Permanente Northern California). Included patients had active health plan membership; had an ED visit for heart failure, pneumonia, cellulitis, urinary tract infection, COVID-19, or anemia; and had their care transitioned to an ATC, ACAH program (Kaiser Permanente Advanced Care at Home), EDOU, or inpatient bed.

Exposure: Treatment venue.

Main outcomes and measures: The main outcomes were care escalation (inpatient admission) for patients treated in an ATC, ACAH program, or EDOU, as well as 7-day ED return visits, 30-day hospitalizations, and 30-day mortality following care completion across all venues. Unadjusted outcome rates are reported.

Results: This study included 26 618 ED encounters (median patient age, 77 years [IQR, 65-85 years]; 52.6% female). Among 22 755 unique patients, 87.4% had 1 encounter, 9.8% had 2 encounters, and 2.8% had more than 2 encounters. There were 728 (2.7%), 880 (3.3%), 5133 (19.3%), and 19 877 (74.7%) encounters in ATC, ACAH, EDOU, and hospital settings, respectively. One-quarter of patients (25.3%) received care in an ATC, ACAH program, or EDOU. Inpatient admission rates were lower for ATC and ACAH encounters than for EDOU encounters (4.3% [95% CI, 2.7%-5.8%], 5.3% [3.8%-6.8%], and 28.0% [26.8%-29.2%], respectively). Rates of 7-day ED visits were similar across venues (ATC: 10.4% [95% CI, 7.8%-12.9%]; ACAH: 5.3% [3.8%-6.8%]; EDOU: 9.2% [8.4%-10.0%]; and hospital: 8.5% [8.1%-8.9%]). In contrast, 30-day mortality and hospitalization rates were lower among ATC, ACAH, and EDOU encounters than in hospital encounters (30-day mortality: 2.1% [95% CI, 1.0%-3.2%], 1.7% [0.8%-2.6%], 2.8% [2.3%-3.2%], and 5.3% [5.0%-5.6%]; and 30-day hospitalization: 11.4% [95% CI, 8.8%-14.1%], 8.3% [6.3%-10.2%], 12.7% [11.7%-13.7%], and 15.3% [14.7%-15.8%], respectively).

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of patients treated in alternative venues of care, one-quarter received care in an ATC, ACAH program, or EDOU. These findings suggest that adoption of novel treatment spaces for appropriately selected patients may allow health systems to focus hospital resources on the patients with the most complex needs.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Accelerated Approvals and Clinical Evidence for Medications for Children
item.description:
Importance: The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) accelerated approval (AA) pathway allows early access to therapies for serious or life-threatening diseases based on surrogate end points reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit. In pediatrics, where evidence generation is challenging, the use and performance of this pathway remain underexamined.

Objective: To characterize preapproval and postapproval studies of drugs granted pediatric AAs.

Design, setting, and participants: This cross-sectional study identified preapproval and postapproval studies for pediatric AAs granted between January 1, 2000, and December 31, 2020. Study characteristics and regulatory outcomes were extracted using publicly available sources, including FDA product labels, approval letters, the postmarketing requirements (PMRs) database, ClinicalTrials.gov, and matched peer-reviewed publications as of August 22, 2026.

Exposures: Granting of pediatric AA.

Main outcomes and measures: Study characteristics and regulatory outcomes, including time from AA to traditional approval.

Results: From 2000 to 2020, the FDA granted AA to 26 drugs for 35 pediatric indications (7 pediatric-only, 6 pediatric extension, and 22 combined pediatric-adult). Most approvals were supported by extrapolation, including pharmacokinetic bridging. A total of 47 PMRs were issued, primarily for efficacy verification (28 [59.6%]), 26 (55.3%) of which were fulfilled, contributing to traditional approval for 22 indications (62.9%) after a median of 58.1 (IQR, 44.5-80.1) months. Pediatric-only indications had the longest conversion times and lowest PMR fulfillment rates, accounting for 3 of 4 cases with delayed PMR fulfillment.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cross-sectional study of pediatric AAs between 2000 and 2020, approval frequently relied on surrogate end points and extrapolation with pharmacokinetic bridging studies, with limited pediatric enrollment. Although confirmatory studies typically verified efficacy within 4 years, pediatric-only indications experienced persistent delays, underscoring ongoing challenges in timely pediatric evidence generation.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: National Trends in Severe Maternal Morbidity by Insurance and Race and Ethnicity
item.description:
Importance: Rates of severe maternal morbidity (SMM) and mortality are rising in the US, disproportionally affecting racial and ethnic minority groups and Medicaid beneficiaries. Contemporary analyses investigating the intersectional impact of insurance and race and ethnicity on SMM are lacking.

Objective: To examine national trends in SMM and maternal mortality across deliveries and evaluate the intersectional association of insurance type and race and ethnicity with these outcomes.

Design, setting, and participants: This serial cross-sectional study used population-based National Inpatient Sample (a 20% stratified sample of hospital discharges) data on delivery hospitalizations from October 1, 2015, to December 31, 2022, in the US, with analyses completed between July 7, 2025, and January 30, 2026.

Exposure: Assessment of insurance (private vs Medicaid) and race and ethnicity independently and cross-classified into 10 intersectional groups.

Main outcomes and measures: Primary outcomes were composite SMM, nontransfusion-only SMM, and mortality. Multivariable logistic regression was used to estimate adjusted odds ratios (AORs) for outcomes across insurance, race and ethnicity, and intersectional groups.

Results: Among 27 341 986 weighted deliveries (mean [SD] maternal age, 29.0 [5.8] years; 6.3% of Asian or Pacific Islander, 16.2% of Black, 22.4% of Hispanic, 0.8% of Native American, and 54.3% of White race and ethnicity), 563 250 (2.1%) were complicated by SMM, 2320 of which (0.4%) resulted in death. From 2015 to 2022, composite SMM rates increased 40.5% (from 175.0 to 245.9 per 10 000 deliveries; P < .001), with 16 of 21 individual complications (76.2%) significantly increasing. Medicaid covered 11 658 119 weighted deliveries (45.5%), and included a greater proportion of Black, Hispanic, and Native American individuals than the privately insured population. Adjusted odds of composite SMM were elevated among all intersectional groups compared with White patients with private insurance (all P < .001). Within each racial and ethnic group, SMM odds were significantly higher with Medicaid vs private insurance (Asian or Pacific Islander: AOR, 1.28 [95% CI, 1.20-1.36]; Black: AOR, 1.13 [95% CI, 1.10-1.17]; Hispanic: AOR, 1.29 [95% CI, 1.24-1.34]; Native American: AOR, 1.44 [95% CI, 1.24-1.67]; White: AOR, 1.23 [95% CI, 1.20-1.26]). Significantly increased odds of mortality were primarily observed for Medicaid-insured Asian or Pacific Islander (AOR, 2.63 [95% CI, 1.25-5.52]), Hispanic (AOR, 1.97 [95% CI, 1.16-3.35]), and White (AOR, 2.15 [95% CI, 1.55-2.99]) patients but not for Medicaid-insured Black patients (AOR, 1.55 [95% CI, 0.99-2.41]).

Conclusions and relevance: This serial cross-sectional study of births in the US found that racial and ethnic minority status was independently associated with elevated odds of SMM. Medicaid enrollment further compounded this risk and was associated with maternal mortality, suggesting underlying structural inequities that accompany Medicaid coverage rather than a direct effect of insurance type. Addressing these structural barriers through policy reform, including equitable reimbursement and expanded preconception coverage, is critical to mitigate these maternal health inequities.

item.title: J Addict Med: Development of an Interprofessional Teamwork Entrustable Professional Activity for Addiction Medicine and Addiction Psychiatry Fellows
item.description:
Background: Substance-use disorders (SUD) require collaborative, multi-specialty care. While graduate medical education (GME) fellowships in addiction medicine (AM) and addiction psychiatry (AP) prepare trainees for interprofessional collaborative care, standard Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education milestones lack a mechanism to directly observe and assess competence in providing interprofessional team-based care.

Objective: To develop and pilot an entrustable professional activity (EPA) focused on interprofessional team-based care applicable to both AM and AP fellowships.

Methods: Using a systematic 3-step consensus process, a multidisciplinary faculty team mapped overlapping AM and AP milestones across 6 Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education core domains to identify those related to interprofessional work. Key functions and a scoring instrument to measure them were developed by an iterative consensus process. The team then drafted an Interprofessional EPA listing foundational milestones and related functions alongside descriptions of expected behaviors at 3 developmental levels.

Results: The EPA was piloted with faculty and fellows. Initial implementation faced barriers regarding faculty uptake due to competing demands. Based on faculty feedback, the EPA was transitioned from a summative scale to a formative tool utilizing narrative summaries to enhance real-time feedback and support milestone reporting.

Conclusions: This EPA provides a structured approach to assess essential, observable interprofessional clinical skills. By shifting to a formative framework, the tool facilitates low-stakes feedback and fosters cross-disciplinary learning. As there is a national push to incorporate EPAs into trainee assessments, this process can inform other residency and fellowship training programs nationally in implementing similar frameworks.

Objectives: This study evaluated the use of addiction consult services and medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD) among hospitalized reproductive-aged women with opioid use diagnoses, examining reach to pregnant women, women admitted to obstetrics, and across race and ethnicity.

Methods: Using electronic health records (2021-2022), we identified admissions among women aged 18-44 with opioid use diagnoses (disorders, poisonings/adverse effects) at 8 New York City public hospitals with addiction consult services. Bayesian hierarchical logistic models estimated associations of being pregnant (vs. not pregnant), admitted to obstetrics (vs. medicine/other departments), and race/ethnicity with consult orders; consult completions; MOUD orders; and MOUD orders among those with completed consults. We report adjusted odds ratios (aOR) and 95% credible intervals (CrIs).

Results: Among 547 eligible admissions (388 patients), 11.7% were pregnant and 9.9% were admitted to obstetrics. Patients were Black (23.5%), Hispanic (33.0%), multiracial/other races (13.7%), and White (26.8%). Compared with medicine/other departments, obstetrics patients had lower odds of a consult order (aOR=0.31; 95% CrI: 0.11-0.78). Black women had lower odds of a consult order (aOR=0.42; 95% CrI: 0.18-0.96) and MOUD (aOR=0.25; 95% CrI: 0.09-0.71) compared to White women.

Conclusions: Findings highlight pregnancy-related differences and racial inequities in addiction consult service and MOUD utilization during hospitalization, underscoring a potential need for stronger obstetrics-addiction collaboration and equity-focused care.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Full-Service Mobile Food Markets and Dietary Quality in Low-Income Housing Communities: A Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Full-service mobile markets, also known as grocery stores on wheels, may improve diet-related outcomes by bringing low-cost, nutritious food to individuals experiencing low incomes and low food access.

Objective: To determine the impact of the full-service Twin Cities Mobile Market on dietary outcomes in low-income communities.

Design, setting, participants: This cluster randomized clinical trial was conducted over 3 waves (January 2022 to October 2025) across 12 public or private subsidized housing sites in the Minneapolis-St. Paul, Minnesota, area. Participants were screened for interest in the mobile market. Follow-up assessments began after 6 months of market service. Analyses were finalized September 2026.

Intervention: Sites were randomized to weekly market service or waiting list control groups.

Main outcomes and measures: Primary outcome: diet quality (Healthy Eating Index-2020 via 24-hour recalls). A priori secondary outcomes: dietary intake (fruit and vegetable, energy, sodium, and percentage of calories from added sugar), food security (18-item US Department of Agriculture Food Security Screening Module), and fruit and vegetable servings procured for the home (validated tracking tool). Adjusted intention-to-treat (ITT) generalized estimating equations were used to assess outcome differences between treatment groups.

Results: Among 262 adults who enrolled in the mobile market study, 242 participants (mean [SD] age, 66.5 [11.5] years; 156 women [64.5%]) across 12 sites completed baseline assessments and were randomized to mobile market service or waiting list control groups. There were 137 individuals (56.6%) who received Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits. Sites had a mean (SD) of 18.2 (4.4) weekly transactions (mean of 110 of 1071 households [10.3%]). Of 109 intervention site participants, 47 individuals (43.1%) shopped at the mobile market 1 or more times in implementation months 5 to 6, while 90 of 94 individuals who reported ever using the market (95.7%) reported that they would recommend the market service. Participant retention was 218 of 242 participants (90.0%). In ITT models, the primary outcome of diet quality (adjusted mean difference, 1.25 [95% CI, -1.60 to 4.10]) among 215 participants and 6 of 7 secondary outcomes (fruit and vegetable, energy, and added sugar intake; food security and food security improvement; fruit and vegetable procurement) were not significantly different between groups. Intervention site participants consumed an adjusted mean difference of 397 mg (95% CI, -636 to -158 mg) less sodium daily compared with participants in the waiting list control group. Main findings were consistent across 4 sensitivity and supplemental analyses, except the per-protocol sensitivity analysis, which found that participants in the intervention group consumed an adjusted mean difference of 2.35% (95% CI, 0.66%-4.04%) more calories from added sugar compared with the control group.

Conclusions and relevance: In this study, satisfaction with the mobile market was high, but the mobile market did not improve diet quality or most outcomes examined. The mobile market was associated with a meaningful sodium reduction that could improve population-level health.
