item.category: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
item.description:
Background: Inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)-containing reliever therapy has demonstrated efficacy in improving asthma outcomes when compared to short-acting beta2-agonists (SABA) alone but remains underutilized. The purpose of this guideline is to provide recommendations surrounding the use of combination ICS-formoterol or ICS+SABA (in combination or separate inhalers) as reliever therapy across the asthma severity spectrum in adolescents and adults.

Methods: The American Thoracic Society clinical practice guideline panel evaluated six research questions in the PICO format addressing the use of ICS-containing reliever therapy across National Asthma Education and Prevention Program (NAEPP) asthma treatment steps 1-5. The methodology team conducted systematic literature reviews and GRADE assessments, which the panel utilized to inform the recommendations for each specific PICO and overall.

Recommendations: In patients at NAEPP steps 1 and 2, the panel made strong recommendations for the use of as-needed-only ICS-SABA or ICS-formoterol over SABA-only therapy, and conditional recommendations over scheduled ICS + as-needed SABA. In patients at NAEPP steps 3-5, the taskforce made a strong recommendation for the use of maintenance-and-reliever therapy (MART) with ICS-formoterol over scheduled ICS-LABA plus as-needed SABA. In patients at NAEPP steps 3-5 who are using scheduled maintenance ICS-LABA, the panel made a conditional recommendation for use of ICS+SABA reliever over SABA reliever. In considering these recommendations, the panel valued the importance of preventing severe exacerbations and considered the risk of SABA-only treatment, as well as ICS and systemic corticosteroid (SCS) exposure.

Conclusions: This clinical practice guideline, informed by systematic reviews and GRADE-based appraisals of PICO-framed evidence, makes these evidence-based recommendations for the safe and effective use of ICS-containing reliever therapy in asthma.

item.title: Crit Care: Coagulopathy and anticoagulation management in adult ECPR patients
item.description:
Extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) has emerged as a lifesaving strategy for refractory cardiac arrest, restoring systemic perfusion when conventional cardiopulmonary resuscitation fails. However, ECPR profoundly disrupts haemostasis, driven by the combined effects of whole-body ischaemia-reperfusion injury, systemic inflammation, endothelial activation, platelet dysfunction, and blood contact with extracorporeal surfaces. Together, these processes create a highly dynamic and unstable thromboinflammatory milieu, marked by the simultaneous risk of thrombosis and life-threatening bleeding. Systemic anticoagulation is required to maintain circuit patency and prevent thromboembolic complications, yet optimal strategies remain uncertain. Haemostasis during ECPR is highly dynamic, shaped by the underlying aetiology of cardiac arrest, patient-specific characteristics, and circuit-related factors. This complexity underscores the limitations of fixed anticoagulation targets and the need for individualized, context-sensitive management guided by continuous clinical and laboratory assessment. Despite the increasing global adoption of ECPR, high-quality evidence to guide anticoagulation practices remains scarce. Current strategies are largely extrapolated from other extracorporeal life support populations, contributing to substantial inter-centre variability. This review synthesizes the available evidence on coagulopathy and anticoagulation in adult patients receiving ECPR and discusses emerging approaches to monitoring and anticoagulation management.

item.title: Crit Care: Distinct transcriptomic signatures discriminate hyperinflammation from immune paralysis in sepsis: a single-cell RNA sequencing study
item.description:
Background: Sepsis is a highly heterogeneous syndrome characterized by variable immune dysregulation states, including hyperinflammation and immunosuppression. Previous immunotherapy attempts in sepsis have largely failed, likely due to a "one-size-fits-all" approach that ignores each patient's immune status. The recent ImmunoSep randomized clinical trial demonstrated that precision immunotherapy guided by the presence of either macrophage activation-like syndrome (MALS) or immune paralysis can improve early organ dysfunction in sepsis patients. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying these immune endotypes remain unclear.

Objectives: To identify the immunological signatures that distinguish MALS and immune paralysis.

Methods: We used single-cell RNA sequencing to profile circulating leukocytes of 6 healthy controls and 16 sepsis patients classified as MALS, immune paralysis or unclassified (when criteria for neither of these two immune endotypes were applicable). Classification was based on surrogate biomarkers ferritin and HLA-DR expression on monocytes. Thereafter, the transcriptional programs of these groups were compared.

Results: Pronounced differences were detected mainly in the transcriptional signature of monocytes from these patients, with a clear distinction between MALS and immune paralysis. Unsupervised clustering analysis revealed the existence of MALS-specific monocyte clusters, as well as one sepsis-specific monocyte cluster that was linked to greater comorbidity burden and may reflect increased clinical vulnerability in sepsis. These findings were validated in two independent cohorts, in which urosepsis was characterized by heterogeneous MALS and immune paralysis monocyte signatures. Moreover, MALS-specific monocyte clusters showed overlapping transcriptional signatures with severe COVID-19.

Conclusions: Our findings shed light on the heterogeneous immune landscape underlying sepsis and provide opportunities for patient stratification for future therapeutic development.

item.title: Crit Care: Differentiated effect of hypothermia versus normothermia after cardiac arrest by neurological status and clinical correlates of ischemic burden
item.description:
Introduction: The optimal temperature target after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remains uncertain, as major randomized trials have not demonstrated a clear benefit of lower-target hypothermia compared with normothermia. Despite this, patients with differing degrees of ischemic burden or early neurological injury may hypothetically respond differently to temperature targets, raising the possibility of heterogeneous treatment effects. This study aimed to determine whether outcomes differ after OHCA with 33 °C versus controlled normothermia (36.0-37.7 °C) according to correlates of ischemic burden and neurological findings at hospital admission.

Methods: This secondary analysis of the TTM and TTM2 trials employed effect-based machine learning to probe for heterogeneous treatment effects. Causal forests and Bayesian additive regression trees (BART) estimated individualized treatment effects (ITE) based on ischemia duration, prehospital factors, and neurological examination findings at hospital admission. Treatment effect modifier variable importance parameter (TEM-VIP) analysis ranked the baseline variables most likely to modify effect. The primary outcome was six-month all-cause mortality, and the secondary outcome was poor functional outcome (modified Rankin scale score 4-6). Primary analyses evaluated potential heterogeneity within each trial, while secondary analyses pooled all participants.

Measurements and main results: All 2789 adult OHCA patients from the trials' primary analyses were included (median age 65 years (IQR 56-73), 79.9% male). Death occurred in 49.4% of patients in the 33 °C group, and in 47.9% in the controlled normothermia group. Variation in six-month mortality ITEs estimated from ischemic burden correlates and initial neurological findings was minimal, and no significant heterogeneity of treatment effect was identified across all methods and analysis populations. In the pooled analysis, estimated conditional mean mortality risk difference ranged from - 1.2% to 2.1% in causal forest (p = 0.99), and from - 0.5% to 1.5% in BART, with posterior probabilities for hypothermia benefit ranging from 42% to 53%. Absolute subgroup estimates in TEM-VIP analysis were small and non-significant. Results were consistent for the six-month functional outcome.

Conclusions: Among TTM and TTM2 participants randomized to 33 °C versus controlled normothermia post-OHCA, no evidence of detectable heterogeneity of treatment effect based on available clinical correlates of ischemic burden or initial neurological findings was identified, with minimal estimated variation in treatment effect.

item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Introduction: Physician-in-Triage (PIT) models may influence diagnostic imaging decisions in the emergency department (ED). We evaluated the association between PIT exposure and imaging utilization among patients with renal colic and examined the influence of physician ultrasound training on imaging selection.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults with an ED diagnosis of renal colic at a single tertiary ED from January 2024 through December 2025. A prespecified lower-risk subgroup included patients aged <51 years with prior nephrolithiasis, no infection, and normal creatinine. The primary exposure was PIT evaluation. Outcomes included computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis (CTAP), point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS), and radiology-performed renal ultrasound (RUS) utilization. Multivariable logistic regression was used to evaluate the association between PIT exposure and each imaging outcome after adjustment for age, gender, emergency severity index, admission, and race.

Results: Of 1041 patients, 596 (57.3%) were exposed to PIT. CTAP utilization was higher among PIT-exposed patients than non-PIT patients (72.9% vs 66.1%; adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.40, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.07-1.85). PIT exposure was associated with lower POCUS utilization (10.3% vs 18.6%; aOR 0.49, 95% CI 0.34-0.70), while RUS utilization was similar (10.1% vs 9.0%; aOR 1.17, 95% CI 0.76-1.79). Overall ultrasound utilization (POCUS or RUS) was also lower among PIT-exposed patients (20.1% vs 26.7%; aOR 0.69, 95% CI 0.51-0.93). In the lower-risk subgroup, PIT exposure remained associated with greater CTAP utilization (63.6% vs 48.1%, p = 0.028) and lower POCUS utilization (14.4% vs 30.4%, p = 0.008). Ultrasound-trained attendings used CTAP less frequently than non-ultrasound-trained attendings (57.8% vs 71.8%; aOR for non-ultrasound-trained physicians 1.86, 95% CI 1.18-2.93).

Conclusion: PIT exposure was associated with greater CTAP and lower ultrasound utilization in patients with renal colic, including among a prespecified lower-risk cohort. Ultrasound-trained physicians used ultrasound more frequently and CTAP less frequently in renal colic patients.

item.title: Resuscitation: Wearable-based automated cardiac arrest detection and alerting: A systematic review
item.description:
Introduction: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remains a leading cause of death worldwide, with survival strongly dependent on rapid recognition and timely emergency care. Wearables capable of automated cardiac arrest detection and alerting may reduce delays to treatment, particularly in unwitnessed arrests.Therefore, this review aims to systematically evaluate the existing evidence on the performance of wearable sensors and algorithms designed for OHCA detection.

Methods: A systematic search was performed using PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, the Cochrane Libraries, forward citation and backward citation to identify all eligible studies up to 22 September 2026. Studies describing non-invasive, intended wearable systems designed to detect OHCA and reporting on their detection performance were included. The methodology and report of the present review are based on recommendations of the PRISMA statement and Cochrane Collaboration. Primary outcome is the sensitivity for cardiac arrest detection. Secondary outcomes include false positives cardiac arrest alerts and specificity. Studies were evaluated using the QUADAS-2 tool.

Results: From 6,344 records screened, 13 publications were included with the number of participants ranging from 18 to 1,423. Wristbands were the most prevalent device type (n=9). Nine studies used photoplethysmography as primary sensor type, with accelerometry as additive sensor modality (n=2). Other sensors used were mechanical plethysmography (n=1), electrocardiography (n=1), sound-based (n=1) and a nonlinear resonant circuit (n=1). Sensitivity ranged between 43.8 and 100%, with ten studies reporting a sensitivity of ≥ 90%. False positives ranged between multiple per day and one per twenty-one user-years.

Discussion: Wearable devices have demonstrated promising sensitivity for detecting cardiac arrest. However, (external) validation and real-life data are scarce, and the sensitivity-false alarm trade-off requires further investigation.

Randomized trials have shown short-term benefit of extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) for refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), but the long-term durability of survival and neurological recovery after hospital discharge remains poorly defined. We performed a retrospective cohort study of consecutive patients discharged alive after ECPR for refractory VT/VF OHCA from two academic centers (University of Minnesota, USA, and Charles University, Prague) from January 2013 through December 2022. The primary outcome was 5-year survival. Secondary outcomes included neurological status by Cerebral Performance Category (CPC) and associations of age and discharge disposition with long-term outcomes. Among 728 patients treated with ECPR, 211 (29.0%) survived to discharge; 138 from Minnesota and 73 from Prague. Median follow-up was 3.9 years; 68 patients (32%) completed 5 years. No patients were lost to follow-up. Among hospital survivors, 76.9% and 67.2% were alive at 1 and 5 years, respectively, with most deaths occurring within 90 days of discharge. CPC 1-2 was present in 78.7% at discharge and remained high among survivors beyond 1 year (93.4%-94.2%). Five-year survival declined by age from 91.6% for those between 18-39 years to 52.9% for >70 years. Discharge disposition also strongly stratified long-term prognosis. Among patients discharged alive after ECPR for refractory OHCA, long-term survival was substantial, with approximately two-thirds alive at 5 years with favorable CPC in most. Younger age and discharge home or to acute rehabilitation identified subgroups with particularly favorable prognosis. These findings support the long-term durability of benefit among selected patients treated within established ECPR systems of care.

item.description:
Background: The clinical meaning of post-resuscitation ST-segment elevation in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients with suspected coronary etiology remains uncertain. We aimed to describe coronary angiographic phenotypes and clinical outcomes according to post-resuscitation ST-segment findings in an angiography-evaluable subset of OHCA survivors with presumed coronary lesion-related arrest.

Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 149 successfully resuscitated OHCA patients admitted to our institution between January 2015 and December 2023, who underwent post-resuscitation coronary angiography and had presumed culprit lesions, defined by integrating angiographic findings with electrocardiographic, echocardiographic, and biomarker data in the clinical context. Patients were classified according to the presence or absence of post-resuscitation ST-segment elevation.

Results: ST-segment elevation was associated with a more acute occlusive coronary phenotype, with more impaired culprit-vessel flow and greater myocardial injury. In contrast, patients without ST-segment elevation more frequently had multivessel disease and chronic total occlusion, suggesting more complex coronary artery disease. Favorable neurological outcome was less frequent with ST-segment elevation in unadjusted analyses, but this association was not independent of pre-hospital factors.

Conclusions: In this selected OHCA subset, post-resuscitation ST-segment elevation was associated with an acute occlusive coronary phenotype and greater myocardial injury, as in non-arrest acute coronary syndromes. However, the absence of ST-segment elevation did not exclude a coronary culprit lesion, so comprehensive coronary assessment is essential. ST-segment elevation was not independently associated with clinical outcomes after adjustment for pre-hospital factors. These findings should be interpreted considering substantial selection inherent to the study population.

Background: Several studies have investigated the diagnostic value of serum procalcitonin (PCT) for pneumonia in patients with acute dyspnea, but results have been inconsistent. This systematic review aimed to determine the diagnostic accuracy of serum PCT for pneumonia in patients with acute dyspnea.

Methods: We searched the PubMed and Web of Science databases to identify studies evaluating the diagnostic accuracy of serum PCT for pneumonia-associated acute dyspnea published before October 1, 2025. The quality of the included studies was assessed using the revised Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies (QUADAS-2). We used a bivariate model to be pooled sensitivity and specificity. The overall diagnostic accuracy was evaluated using a summary receiver operating characteristic curve (sROC). Deek's test was used to assess publication bias.

Results: We included 6 studies involving 2341 patients (576 with pneumonia and 1765 without). Serum PCT's pooled sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing pneumonia-related acute dyspnea were 0.67 (95% CI: 0.58-0.75) and 0.76 (95% CI: 0.67-0.83), respectively. The area under the sROC curve (AUC) was 0.77 (95% CI: 0.73-0.80). The positive likelihood ratio (PLR) and negative likelihood ratio (NLR) were 2.8 (95% CI: 2.0-3.8) and 0.44 (95% CI: 0.34-0.56), respectively. The diagnostic odds ratio (DOR) was 6 (95% CI: 4-10). The included studies showed no significant publication bias.

Conclusions: Serum PCT has only moderate diagnostic value for pneumonia-related acute dyspnea and is insufficient to confirm or exclude pneumonia when used alone.

item.title: Ann Intern Med: Decompression With or Without Fusion Across Subgroups With Degenerative Lumbar Spondylolisthesis : A Target Trial Emulation
item.description:
Background: Randomized trials have shown limited benefits and increased risks of adding spinal fusion surgery to decompression for degenerative spondylolisthesis. Decompression with fusion has increasingly been used in the United States.

Objective: To examine the comparative effectiveness of decompression with fusion versus decompression alone for patient subgroups.

Design: Cohort study using the target trial framework.

Setting: Norwegian Registry for Spine Surgery and nested NORDSTEN-DS (Norwegian degenerative spondylolisthesis and spinal stenosis) randomized trial.

Patients: Adults aged 18 to 80 years with lumbar degenerative spondylolisthesis and symptomatic back or leg pain lasting at least 3 months.

Intervention: Lumbar spinal decompression surgery with fusion versus lumbar spinal decompression surgery alone.

Measurements: The primary outcomes were Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) score and reoperation at 12 months. Linear regression models with inverse probability weighting to control for baseline confounding were used to obtain effect estimates with 95% CIs for decompression with fusion versus decompression alone for prespecified subgroups, including sex, age, smoking, body mass index (BMI), back pain intensity, and American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) grade.

Results: Of 2252 patients, 236 were in the NORDSTEN-DS randomized trial. The mean age was 66 years, and 1576 (70%) women were included. A total of 1446 patients had decompression alone, and 806 had decompression with fusion; respective unadjusted baseline ODI scores were 38.9 (SD, 14.9) and 41.4 (SD, 14.7). At 12 months, the ODI score was 22.3 (95% CI, 15.5 to 29.1) for decompression alone and 20.0 (CI, 13.9 to 26.2) for decompression with fusion; the mean difference was 2.2 (CI, -1.6 to 6.1). In exploratory analyses, the ODI score was worse for decompression with fusion for men with BMI of 30 kg/m2 or higher. Reoperation risk at 12 months did not differ.

Limitation: Possible residual confounding.

Conclusion: Patient subgroups did not have differential effects from the addition of fusion to decompression at 12 months.

item.title: Ann Intern Med: Timing of Long COVID Improvement in Prospectively Followed RECOVER-Adult Participants
item.description:
Background: Long COVID (LC) is widespread; however, limited information has been reported on the likelihood that symptoms remit over time.

Objective: To evaluate the likelihood of improvement among persons with likely LC.

Design: Prospective, multisite cohort study (RECOVER-Adult [Researching COVID to Enhance Recovery]).

Setting: 83 U.S.-based sites across 33 states; Washington, DC; and Puerto Rico.

Participants: 1019 persons in RECOVER-Adult with likely LC (LC Research Index [LCRI] ≥11) 12 months after first SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Measurements: The primary outcome was time until 2 consecutive study visits with LCRI less than 11. Secondary outcomes were time until LCRI measure reduced 50% or more and quality of life was good or better, and LCRI decreased to 0. Unadjusted estimates of cumulative incidence and adjusted marginal cumulative incidence by age, sex, SARS-CoV-2 wave, and LC subtype were reported across all follow-up time points.

Results: An estimated 36.2% (95% CI, 33.0% to 39.5%) met the primary outcome by 24 months after infection, and 50.1% (CI, 46.1% to 54.0%) met the primary outcome by 36 months. An estimated 56.4% (CI, 52.2% to 60.4%) and 26.9% (CI, 23.3% to 30.5%), respectively, met the 2 secondary outcomes by 36 months. Among persons who still reported likely LC at 18 months and 24 months after first infection, relative timing of subsequent symptom improvement was similar.

Limitation: Findings in this observational cohort are interpretable in a population with prevalent likely LC and do not address causal relationships between individual characteristics and symptom improvement.

Conclusion: Among persons with likely LC 12 months after initial SARS-CoV-2 infection, one half experience meaningful reductions in symptoms by 36 months, whereas a quarter experience complete remission of symptoms. These findings underscore both the potential for natural recovery and the urgent need for placebo-controlled therapeutic intervention trials.

Primary funding source: National Institutes of Health.

item.title: J Addict Med: Examination of Infant Sex Differences in Neonatal Opioid Withdrawal Syndrome Severity After In-Utero Buprenorphine Exposure in the MOMS Clinical Trial
item.description:
Objectives: Neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome (NOWS) severity is influenced by several clinical factors; however, the association with infant sex is poorly understood. We examined the association between infant sex and NOWS severity in a cohort of buprenorphine-exposed infants.

Methods: This was a secondary analysis of the MOMS clinical trial (NCT03918850). Regression models evaluated the association between infant sex and NOWS severity measures, including (1) receipt of any pharmacologic treatment, (2) opioid treatment days, (3) adjunctive medication treatment, (4) length of hospital stay (LOS), and (5) LOS related to NOWS.

Results: There were 135 infants (67 male, 68 female). There were no significant differences in demographics or medical comorbidities by infant sex. Methamphetamine and phencyclidine exposures were positively associated with receipt of any pharmacologic treatment, and phencyclidine with longer LOS. Breastfeeding was associated with decreased receipt of any pharmacologic treatment and shorter total LOS, and preterm delivery and NICU admission with longer total LOS. In final regression models, NOWS severity did not differ by infant sex.

Conclusions: Infant sex was not statistically associated with NOWS severity measures within this buprenorphine-exposed cohort. Meta-analyses are needed to better understand the relationship between infant sex and NOWS.

item.title: N Engl J Med: TAVR in Patients with Moderate Aortic Stenosis with At-Risk Features
item.category: The New England journal of medicine
item.description:
Background: For patients with moderate aortic stenosis, current guidelines recommend clinical surveillance with echocardiographic assessment every 1 or 2 years. Whether transcatheter aortic-valve replacement (TAVR) will improve outcomes in these patients remains unknown.

Methods: We conducted an international, open-label, randomized trial to evaluate whether TAVR will result in better outcomes than clinical surveillance among patients with moderate aortic stenosis with at least one at-risk feature (i.e., a symptom or structural or functional abnormality that has been shown to be associated with faster disease progression or adverse cardiovascular outcomes). The patients were assigned in a 1:1 ratio to undergo transfemoral TAVR with a balloon-expandable valve or clinical surveillance. The primary effectiveness end point was a composite of death from any cause or a heart-failure event with or without hospitalization at 2 years. Superiority testing was performed in the intention-to-treat population.

Results: A total of 744 patients underwent randomization: 373 patients were assigned to the TAVR group and 371 to the clinical-surveillance group. The mean age of patients was 78 years, 39.1% were women, and 45.6% were at low surgical risk. The mean aortic-valve area was 1.2 cm2, and the mean aortic-valve peak velocity was 3.3 m per second. At 2 years, the Kaplan-Meier estimate of the percentage of patients with a primary effectiveness end-point event was 16.7% in the TAVR group and 23.9% in the clinical-surveillance group (risk difference, -7.2 percentage points; 95% confidence interval, -13.1 to -1.3; P = 0.02 for superiority). The Kaplan-Meier estimate of the percentage of patients who died from any cause was 8.4% in the TAVR group and 7.3% in the clinical-surveillance group; the estimates for a heart-failure event were 10.8% and 19.0%, respectively. The incidence of procedure-related adverse events did not differ meaningfully between the patients in the TAVR group and those in the clinical-surveillance group who underwent aortic-valve replacement.

Conclusions: Among patients with moderate aortic stenosis and at-risk features, a strategy of TAVR was superior to clinical surveillance in lowering the incidence of death or a heart-failure event at 2 years. (Funded by Edwards Lifesciences; PROGRESS ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04889872.).

item.title: JAMA: Antithrombotic Therapy After Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion: The SIMPLAAFY Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Following a left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) procedure, antithrombotic therapy is administered to safely allow time for device endothelialization. However, the optimal postimplant antithrombotic regimen is unknown.

Objective: To determine if either reduced-dose non-vitamin K oral anticoagulants (NOACs) or aspirin alone are noninferior to dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) for the composite clinical end point of death, stroke, systemic embolism, or major bleeding through 6 months post LAAC.

Design, setting, and participants: This open-label, 3-group, multicenter clinical trial randomized 1857 patients between October 2024 and December 2025 at 87 US investigational sites, with the final 6-month follow-up in July 2026. Enrolled patients had nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, underwent successful LAAC, and were eligible for all 3 regimens.

Interventions: Patients were randomly allocated 1:1:1 to DAPT for 6 months followed by aspirin (n = 624), a reduced-dose NOAC for 3 months followed by aspirin (n = 620), or aspirin alone for 12 months (n = 613).

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was the 6-month composite of all-cause death, stroke, systemic embolism, or major bleeding. Noninferiority was tested in the primary analysis population with a 1-sided Farrington-Manning test (α = .025). Bleeding and 45-day device-related thrombus rates were exploratory without multiplicity adjustment.

Results: The cohort had a mean age of 76 (SD, 8) years, 42.9% were female, the mean CHA2DS2-VASc score was 4.2 (SD, 1.3), and 68.0% had paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. The primary outcome occurred in 41 patients (6.9%) with DAPT vs 31 (5.1%) with a reduced-dose NOAC (risk ratio, 0.75 [95% CI, 0.48-1.18]; risk difference, -1.7 percentage points; 97.5% upper bound, 1.2) and 20 (3.3%) with aspirin alone (risk ratio, 0.49 [95% CI, 0.29-0.82]; risk difference, -3.5 percentage points; 97.5% upper bound, -0.8). Both monotherapy strategies met noninferiority criteria (P < .001 for noninferiority for both). Major bleeding was 4.5% with DAPT, 2.7% with reduced-dose NOACs, and 1.7% with aspirin alone; clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding was 8.7%, 4.8%, and 3.8%, respectively. Device-related thrombus was observed in 3.4%, 0.9%, and 2.7%, respectively.

Conclusions and relevance: Both reduced-dose NOACs and aspirin alone were noninferior to DAPT for 6-month outcomes after uncomplicated LAAC.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06521463.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Caring Contacts and Suicidality Among American Indian and Alaska Native Communities: A Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: For American Indian and Alaska Native communities, connectedness and belonging are strengths that may reduce suicide risk.

Objective: To evaluate the effectiveness of culturally-adapted Caring Contacts combined with optimal available resources (intervention) compared with optimal available resources alone (control) in reducing suicidal ideation, suicide attempts, and suicide-related hospitalizations.

Design, setting, and participants: The CARE study was a blinded, 2-group randomized clinical trial conducted between May 2018 and September 2023 among 5 American Indian and Alaska Native communities in Alaska, the Northern Plains, and the Southern Plains, including 4 tribal communities and 1 tribal health organization. Participants were English-speaking adults (age ≥18 years) self-identifying as American Indian or Alaska Native with active suicidality. Analysis was conducted January through April 2024.

Intervention: Caring Contacts is a low-cost intervention via brief, nondemanding messages exclusively focused on expressing care and interest sent by text message or greeting card on a pre-determined schedule over 12 months.

Main outcomes and measures: Outcomes included suicidal ideation in the past month (measured using the Suicidal Ideation Questionnaire-Junior [SIQ-Jr]), number of suicide attempts, and suicide-related hospitalizations over 12 months. Retention of active suicidality at follow-up was added as an additional outcome.

Results: Of 1390 individuals prescreened for eligibility, 1202 consented and were screened for eligibility, and 709 (457 [64.5%] female; mean [SD] age, 35.4 [11.5] years) were enrolled and randomized, including 357 participants in the control group and 352 participants in the Caring Contacts intervention. Most participants (549 [77.4%]) self-identified as American Indian or Alaska Native only, and 160 participants (22.6%) as American Indian or Alaska Native plus another racial group. More than half of participants (392 [55.3%]) were never married. The mean (SD) SIQ-Jr score at baseline was 42.0 (13.8), and 604 participants (85.2%) had ever made a suicide attempt. Overall, 454 participants (64.0%) provided 12-month follow-up data. Between baseline and the 12-month follow-up, both groups showed significant reductions in suicidal ideation (mean [SD] score: Caring Contacts, 41.4 [13.7] vs 22.7 [15.3]; enhanced usual care, 42.5 [13.9] vs 23.1 [14.5]) and participants with a past-year suicide attempt (Caring Contacts, 169 of 352 participants [48.0%] vs 34/240 participants [14.2%]; enhanced usual care 155 of 357 participants [43.4%] vs 39 of 238 participants [16.4%]); however, no statistically significant between-group differences were found.

Conclusions and relevance: In this randomized clinical trial of culturally adapted Caring Contacts among American Indian or Alaska Native adults with active suicidality, Caring Contacts did not improve suicidal outcomes beyond optimal available resources alone. Similar improvements in both groups may reflect regression to the mean, the therapeutic impact of compassionate baseline engagement with supportive community staff, or the active components of optimal available resources. Further research should explore these dynamics and other culturally grounded interventions.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT02825771.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Cost-Effectiveness of Remote Symptom Monitoring During Adjuvant Endocrine Therapy in Breast Cancer
item.description:
Importance: Adjuvant endocrine therapy (AET) reduces recurrence and mortality for women with early-stage hormone receptor-positive breast cancer, yet long-term adherence is suboptimal, largely due to treatment-related symptoms. Remote patient monitoring (RPM) is a potential strategy to improve symptom management, but evidence of its cost-effectiveness is limited.

Objective: To evaluate the cost-effectiveness of RPM for women prescribed AET for early-stage breast cancer.

Design, setting, and participants: This economic evaluation used data from the THRIVE trial, which randomized adult women initiating AET to an application (app), the app with tailored feedback, or enhanced usual care (EUC) at a large cancer center with 14 clinics from November 15, 2018, to June 11, 2021. The intervention lasted 6 months, and participants were followed up for 12 months (completed September 19, 2022). Each of the 2 interventions was compared with EUC, with uncertainty assessed using probabilistic sensitivity analyses. Data analyses were performed from February 1, 2025, to September 2, 2026.

Main outcomes and measures: Primary outcomes included costs, which were captured during the 12-month study period from a societal perspective, including medical costs, patient time and travel costs, clinician time costs responding to alerts, and app costs; quality-adjusted life years (QALYs), derived from patient-reported 12-item Short Form Health Survey scores; incremental cost-effectiveness ratios; and incremental net monetary benefit.

Results: Of 304 participants randomized, 214 had complete data. The mean (SD) age was 58.9 (10.8) years. Mean (SD) total costs were highest for the EUC arm ($11 596.10 [$30 231.95]) compared with the app arm ($6682.15 [$12 963.34]; difference, -$4913.95 [95% CI, -$12 864.27 to $3036.37]) and app plus feedback arm ($11 407.85 [$47 068.42]; difference, -$188.25 [95% CI, -$12 830.16 to $12 453.66]). The mean (SD) estimated QALYs were similar across arms (app, 0.79 [012]; app plus feedback, 0.78 [0.13]; EUC, 0.78 [0.12]). This results in an incremental net monetary benefit of $5813.95 (95% uncertainty interval [UI], -$1860.00 to $16 492.58) for app group and $88.25 (95% UI, -$14 781.73 to $13 849.34) for the app plus feedback group at $100 000 per QALY. Probabilistic sensitivity analyses suggest that the app intervention had a 68.2% to 78.1% probability of being cost-effective compared with EUC across a willingness-to-pay threshold of $0 to $200 000 per QALY, while the app plus feedback intervention had a 53.6% to 70.8% probability of being cost-effective.

Conclusions and relevance: In this economic evaluation of RPM for women receiving AET, app-only RPM showed lower costs with similar QALY compared with EUC. Its simpler design may also be more readily scalable than the app plus feedback intervention, supporting its potential as a pragmatic, value-based supportive care strategy in oncology.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Protein Biomarkers of Lung Cancer Risk Among Individuals Who Never Smoked
item.description:
Importance: Approximately one-quarter of lung cancers occur in people who never smoked (PWNS). For smoking-associated lung cancer, blood-based protein biomarkers can improve risk assessment.

Objective: To identify protein biomarkers for lung cancer among PWNS.

Design, setting, and participants: This nested case-control study from 4 cohorts in the Lung Cancer Cohort Consortium (LC3) was conducted for discovery to identify proteins, and a cohort study was conducted using data in the UK Biobank for replication. Participants were from the US, China, and the United Kingdom and donated blood samples between 1996 and 2010. Lung cancer case-control pairs of PWNS from 4 cohorts in the LC3 were matched by cohort, age, sex, and blood collection date. In addition, 49 291 participants in the UK Biobank were included. Data were analyzed from March 2024 to May 2025.

Exposure: A total of 2821 circulating proteins measured in prediagnostic blood samples collected up to 5 years before lung cancer diagnosis for cases.

Main outcomes and measures: Primary measures were odds ratios (ORs) for discovery and hazard ratios (HRs) for replication.

Results: Among 180 case-control pairs of PWNS (360 participants) in the 4 LC3 cohorts, 256 participants (71.1%) were female, and the median (IQR) age at enrollment was 66 (55-70) years. In LC3, using a false discovery rate-adjusted P value threshold of .05, 2 proteins were identified as being associated with lung cancer among PWNS: carcinoembryonic antigen-related cell adhesion molecule 5 (CEACAM5) (OR, 1.65 [95% CI, 1.31-2.09]) and CEACAM6 (OR, 1.72 [95% CI, 1.33-2.22]). Associations for both proteins were successfully replicated among participants analyzed regardless of smoking history across 5 years of follow-up in the UK Biobank (CEACAM5: HR, 1.92 [95% CI, 1.66-2.22]; CEACAM6: HR, 1.86 [95% CI,1.59-2.16]). The correlation between CEACAM5 and CEACAM6 was weak (Pearson ρ = 0.25 in the LC3); therefore, both proteins maintained associations with high relative risks after mutual adjustment. For 36 proteins previously identified as robust markers of smoking-related lung cancer, most showed no evidence of an association among PWNS (median OR, 1.47 [IQR, 1.38-1.61] vs 1.01 [IQR, 0.94-1.13] in smoking-related vs nonsmoking lung cancer).

Conclusions and relevance: In this nested case-control study, 2 proteins were identified, CEACAM5 and CEACAM6, that were associated with lung cancer in PWNS. Larger studies are needed to evaluate whether there are additional biomarkers associated with lung cancer in PWNS and whether they can identify PWNS with high lung cancer risk.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Moral Distress Among Abortion-Providing Clinicians After the US Supreme Court Dobbs Decision
item.description:
Importance: Moral distress among abortion-providing clinicians could lead to burnout and attrition from the workforce, worsening reproductive care disparities.

Objective: To describe situations associated with moral distress among abortion-providing clinicians since the US Supreme Court's Dobbs v Jackson Women's Health Organization decision across a range of policy environments.

Design, setting, and participants: For this qualitative study, purposive sampling was conducted from May to December 2023 through listservs and snowball sampling across the US. Participants were clinicians providing abortion care in the US in the year following Dobbs. Data were analyzed from March 2024 to April 2025.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was determining which situations were associated with moral distress in both protective and restrictive abortion policy environments. Deductive and inductive coding approaches were used to analyze open-ended responses.

Results: Of 310 respondents completing the full survey (271 women [87.7%]; 132 aged 36-45 years [43.6%]), 160 (51.6%) responded to the optional open-ended question. The 160 respondents described situations associated with moral distress in state policy environments that were both protective and restrictive of abortion. Through thematic analysis, 3 main themes of situations associated with moral distress were identified: (1) bans prohibiting conscientious provision of abortion care; (2) forced adjustments to medical practice, including being forced to provide inaccurate information, substandard care, or to limit care due to resource scarcity; and (3) distress related to the broader national environment.

Conclusions and relevance: In this qualitative study, clinicians in both abortion-protective and abortion-restrictive environments reported situations associated with moral distress. item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Functional Connectivity at Birth and Longitudinal Neurocognitive Development in Very Preterm Infants
item.description:
Importance: Understanding how neonatal functional connectivity at birth is associated with later cognitive performance in infants born very preterm (VPT) may help identify early neuroimaging markers of neurodevelopment.

Objective: To examine the associations between functional connectivity at birth and cognitive performance at age 2 and 3 years in children born VPT.

Design, setting, and participants: This prospective cohort study included infants born VPT (gestational age ≤32 weeks) from 5 level III and IV neonatal intensive care units in the greater Cincinnati, Ohio, area between September 16, 2016, and November 19, 2019. Maternal, pregnancy, delivery, and infant clinical data were collected from birth through discharge from the neonatal intensive care unit. Participants underwent magnetic resonance imaging at full-term-equivalent age at Cincinnati Children's Hospital using the same scanner. Image preprocessing and statistical analyses for this study were conducted between January 25, 2025, and July 30, 2026.

Main outcomes and measures: Cognitive outcomes were assessed at corrected age 2 and 3 years using the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, Third Edition and the Differential Ability Scales, Second Edition, respectively. Functional connectivity was measured within and between the default mode network (DMN), somatomotor network (SMN), dorsal attention network (DAN), frontoparietal control network, visual network (VIS), and cingulo-opercular network (CO). Associations between neonatal functional connectivity and longitudinal cognitive outcomes were examined using a bayesian hierarchical linear mixed-effects model.

Results: A total of 257 infants born VPT (mean [SD] gestational age, 29.2 [2.5] weeks; 132 male [51.4%]) were included in the final longitudinal analysis. Stronger neonatal connectivity involving the DMN was positively associated with cognitive performance, including intra-DMN (0.23; 95% credible interval [CrI], 0.06-0.39) and DMN connections with the frontoparietal control network (0.24; 95% CrI, 0.07-0.40), SMN (0.20; 95% CrI, 0.02-0.37), VIS (0.32; 95% CrI, 0.13-0.51), and CO (0.39; 95% CrI, 0.21-0.56). Positive associations were also observed for SMN-VIS (0.27; 95% CrI, 0.12-0.43) and SMN-CO (0.26; 95% CrI, 0.09-0.44) connectivity. The SMN-VIS was the only connection showing a difference between assessments, with a less pronounced association at 3 years than at 2 years (interaction, -0.09; 95% CrI, -0.20 to <0.01).

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of infants born VPT, neonatal functional network organization was associated with cognitive performance at corrected age 2 and 3 years. The findings highlight the relevance of distributed connectivity involving the DMN and SMN to later cognitive outcomes and support further investigation of neonatal functional connectivity as an early marker of neurodevelopment.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Racial and Ethnic Differences in Access to Alzheimer Special Care Units After Hospitalization
item.description:
Importance: Older adults with dementia often need nursing home care after hospitalization.

Objective: To examine whether Black and Hispanic patients have different access to Alzheimer disease special care units (ASCUs) after hospital discharge compared with White patients.

Design, setting, and participants: This was a retrospective cohort study of 100% Medicare fee-for-service claims from January 2018 to February 2020. Participants were Medicare beneficiaries with a prior diagnosis of dementia who were hospitalized or admitted to nursing homes from January 2018 to August 2019. Data analyses were performed from January to July 2026.

Exposure: The race and ethnicity of a patient.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was long-term care admission to a nursing home with an ASCU. An unadjusted logistic regression, an unadjusted 2-level (patient-hospital) model, and a multivariable 2-level model were conducted to assess racial and ethnic differences in long-term care admission to a facility with an ASCU and whether patient and hospital characteristics could explain the differences.

Results: Of the 1 428 849 patients, 130 125 (9.11%) were Black, 77 868 (5.45%) were Hispanic, 1 164 829 (81.52%) were non-Hispanic White, 56 027 (3.92%) were of other races (American Indian or Alaska Native, Asian, and Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander), 839 328 (58.74%) were female, and 1 075 171 (75.25%) were aged 75 years or older. A total of 122 654 patients (8.58%) became long-term care residents within 6 months of hospital discharge, and 19 313 patients (1.35%) were admitted to facilities with an ASCU. In the unadjusted logistic model, Black (relative risk [RR], 0.69; 95% CI, 0.65-0.73) and Hispanic (RR, 0.48; 95% CI, 0.44-0.53) patients had lower probabilities of long-term care admission in a facility with ASCU than White patients. After controlling for the clustering of patients in a hospital, the RR substantially increased to 0.94 (95% CI, 0.88-0.99) for Black patients and 0.78 (95% CI, 0.71-0.85) for Hispanic patients. Further controlling for patient and hospital characteristics slightly reduced these RRs. Disparities for Black patients (RR, 0.89; 95% CI, 0.84-0.95), but not Hispanic patients (RR, 0.93; 95% CI, 0.84-1.02), were also observed in the subcohort of Medicare beneficiaries who became long-term care residents.

Conclusions and relevance: The findings of this cohort study suggest that disparities in access to specialized dementia care occur mostly because patients from minoritized racial and ethnic groups are treated at hospitals with low rates of discharge to ASCUs. Efforts to improve dementia care access should focus on enhancing hospital discharge planning and addressing the extra barriers faced by female patients.

item.title: JAMA Intern Med: Surveillance Mammography and Second Primary Breast Cancer Diagnosis Among Older Women With a History of Breast Cancer
item.description:
Importance: Although surveillance mammography is commonly performed among older women, whether this practice improves clinical outcomes in this population is uncertain.

Objective: To evaluate the association between surveillance mammography and second primary breast cancer stage at diagnosis among older women with a history of breast cancer.

Design, setting, and participants: This retrospective longitudinal cohort study used Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results Program-Medicare data. Women with nonmetastatic breast cancer that was diagnosed from 2004 to 2008 at 67 years or older who had a surveillance mammogram at approximately 5 years after diagnosis were included. Analyses used cause-specific hazard models with inverse probability of treatment weighting to estimate the risk of stage-specific second primary breast cancer among women who continued surveillance mammography and those who did not. Analyses were stratified by hormone receptor (HR) status of the initial breast cancer. Follow-up continued until second breast cancer diagnosis, death, or end of the study (December 2021). Analyses were performed between November 2025 and August 2026.

Exposure: Continued surveillance mammography more than 5 years after initial diagnosis.

Main outcomes and measures: Stage-specific cumulative incidence of a second primary breast cancer, categorized as in situ, localized, or advanced (regional or distant).

Results: Among 9888 women (mean [SD] age, 81.1 [5.5] years; 387 Hispanic [3.9%], 514 non-Hispanic Black [5.1%], and 8514 White individuals [86.1%]), 8055 (81.4%) had in situ or localized disease and 7621 (76.9%) had HR-positive tumors at initial diagnosis. Overall, 7940 women (80.3%) continued surveillance at cohort entry. Advanced second primary breast cancer was rare, and incidence did not differ among those who continued surveillance and those who did not (cumulative incidence, 1.65% vs 2.15%; hazard ratio, 0.76; 95% CI, 0.46-1.26). Results were similar in subgroups of women with initial HR-positive and HR-negative breast cancer.

Conclusions and relevance: The results of this cohort study suggest that among older survivors of breast cancer, continued surveillance mammography was not associated with a reduced risk of advanced second primary breast cancer. The absolute risk of advanced cancer was low, and surveillance decisions should be individualized given the potential burdens of continued surveillance.

item.title: Intensive Care Med: Individualized treatment effects of high flow nasal oxygen in immunocompromised patients
item.description:
Rationale: High flow nasal oxygen (HFNO) has become a common first-line practice for acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (ARF). In immunocompromised patients, ARF is the leading cause of ICU admission, yet a randomized trial found no overall benefit of HFNO in this population.

Objectives: To assess whether baseline characteristics influence HFNO's effectiveness in preventing invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) in immunocompromised patients with ARF.

Methods: A causal forest machine-learning algorithm was derived in the HIGH trial (776 patients randomized to HFNO or conventional oxygen) to predict the HFNO effects on day-28 IMV incidence. Patients with a "do-not-intubate" order (n = 72) were excluded. Model performance was validated through 500 bootstrap iterations and patients were categorized into terciles based on predicted HFNO benefit. Transportability of the model was assessed in an independent observational cohort (818 patients).

Main results: Among the 704 participants, HFNO's average effect on day-28 IMV was not significant. However, substantial heterogeneity in treatment responses was identified (predicted benefit: from 20.2% [IQR 15.5%-23.9%] absolute IMV risk reduction with HFNO to 7.4% risk reduction [2.9%-11.2%] with conventional oxygen). Patients with the highest predicted benefit were older, more frequently solid organ transplant recipients, less neutropenic, more severely hypoxemic/tachycardic, but with lower non-respiratory sequential organ failure assessment (SOFA) scores. In this subgroup, HFNO was associated with a significant lower incidence of IMV. In the observational cohort, the benefit-ranking performance was preserved, although absolute effect estimates were less calibrated.

Conclusions: These results suggest HFNO might benefit specific immunocompromised patients with ARF. Further prospective studies are needed to validate these findings.

item.title: Intensive Care Med: Establishing curriculum priorities for intensive care recovery education: an international Delphi study
item.description:
Purpose: To effectively support recovery, intensive care unit (ICU) clinicians require training to identify patients at risk of post-intensive care syndrome and implement interventions during and after ICU admission. This study aimed to identify and prioritise curriculum topics for educating interprofessional ICU clinicians on evidence-based ICU recovery care across the continuum of critical illness.

Methods: A two-round e-Delphi study followed by a structured consensus meeting endorsed by the European Society of Intensive Care Medicine (ESICM) was conducted. A steering committee generated an initial list of curriculum topics. In round 1, participants rated topic importance (9-point Likert scale) and suggested additional topics. In round 2, they rated newly identified topics and ranked priorities. Topics reaching consensus (≥70% rating as critical [7-9]; ≤15% rating as not important [1-3]) were discussed during the final consensus meeting.

Results: Participants' mean age was 43.5 (±10.5) years and they were predominantly female (n = 90, 66.7%). Priority topics included early mobilisation during ICU admission, post-intensive care syndrome, delirium prevention and management, implementation of the ABCDEF bundle, and cognitive support and rehabilitation. The final set of learning modules for a future curriculum was established.

Conclusion: Priority topics and learning modules for an expert-developed curriculum framework for ICU recovery were established with interprofessional ICU clinicians through a structured international consensus process with moderate levels of participant retention between the two Delphi rounds and full consensus agreement among experts. This framework may support in delivering recovery-focused care across the continuum of critical illness.

item.title: Intensive Care Med: Sodium bicarbonate therapy for metabolic acidosis in critically ill patients: a Bayesian systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
item.description:
Purpose: To evaluate the effects of sodium bicarbonate therapy on mortality and renal outcomes in critically ill adults with metabolic acidosis.

Methods: We performed a systematic review and Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing intravenous sodium bicarbonate with placebo or usual care in adult intensive care unit patients with metabolic acidosis. MEDLINE, Embase and CENTRAL were searched from inception to December 2025, with an updated search on 2 April 2026. The primary outcome was short-term all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included renal replacement therapy (RRT) initiation, 90-day mortality, RRT-free days, vasopressor-free days, intensive care unit and hospital length of stay and adverse events.

Results: Four RCTs including 1544 patients were analysed. Sodium bicarbonate did not show a clear short-term mortality benefit (RR 0.94, 95% CrI 0.73-1.22), with a posterior probability of benefit of 72.1%. For RRT initiation, sodium bicarbonate was associated with a lower risk (RR 0.74, 95% CrI 0.59-0.98), with a posterior probability of benefit of 97.2%. Effects on other outcomes were small or imprecise, and no consistent safety signal was identified.

Conclusion: Current randomised evidence does not demonstrate a clear survival benefit from sodium bicarbonate therapy in critically ill adults with metabolic acidosis, but suggests a high probability of reducing RRT initiation. Further trials should define the patients most likely to benefit. PROSPERO registration: CRD420251246519.

item.description:
Background: Intravascular ultrasound (IVUS)-guided percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) improves clinical outcomes. Coronary computed tomographic angiography (CCTA) provides anatomical and physiological information before cardiac catheterization that may enable PCI planning. Data regarding the use of CCTA-guided PCI as compared with IVUS-guided PCI with respect to clinical outcomes are lacking.

Methods: In this investigator-initiated, international, open-label, randomized, noninferiority trial with blinded end-point adjudication, we randomly assigned patients with a clinical indication for revascularization, at least one epicardial lesion with a diameter stenosis of more than 70%, and a fractional flow reserve derived from CCTA of 0.80 or less in a 1:1 ratio to a CCTA-guided or IVUS-guided PCI strategy. The primary end point was target-vessel failure, defined as a composite of death from cardiac causes, target-vessel myocardial infarction, or ischemia-driven target-vessel revascularization, at 12 months. The noninferiority margin for the absolute risk difference was 4.5 percentage points, with a prespecified hierarchical testing strategy for superiority.

Results: A total of 1105 patients underwent randomization: 556 to the CCTA-guided PCI group and 549 to the IVUS-guided PCI group. The median age of the patients was 65 years, and 21.7% were women. At 12 months, target-vessel failure had occurred in 23 patients (4.1%) in the CCTA-guided PCI group and in 25 patients (4.6%) in the IVUS-guided PCI group (risk difference, -0.42 percentage points; 95% confidence interval, -2.82 to 1.99; P<0.001 for noninferiority; P = 0.73 for superiority). A total of 6 patients in the CCTA-guided PCI group and 9 patients in the IVUS-guided PCI group had clinical procedural complications.

Conclusions: A CCTA-guided PCI strategy was noninferior to IVUS-guided PCI with respect to target-vessel failure at 12 months. (Funded by GE HealthCare and Heartflow; P4 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05253677.).

item.title: Crit Care: Accelerating tracheostomy decannulation with intermittent oro-esophageal feeding in neurogenic dysphagia: a multicenter randomized controlled trial
item.description:
Background: Neurogenic dysphagia frequently constitutes a major barrier to decannulation for tracheostomized patients. Conventional nasogastric tube (NGT) feeding may promote disuse atrophy of swallowing musculature and persistent aspiration risk. Intermittent oro-esophageal tube (IOE) feeding, a physiologically oriented modality mimicking natural swallowing, may accelerate decannulation, yet high-quality evidence is lacking.

Methods: In this multicenter randomized controlled trial conducted at three tertiary academic centers in China, tracheostomized adults with neurogenic dysphagia were randomly assigned 1:1 to IOE or NGT. All participants received standardized pharmacological treatment, pulmonary rehabilitation, and structured swallowing training, and entered an institutional decannulation protocol with predefined readiness criteria. The primary outcome was time from protocol entry to actual decannulation. Secondary outcomes included the 30-day successful decannulation rate, nutritional indices, swallowing function, and swallowing-related quality of life. Outcome assessors and statisticians were blinded to allocation. Analyses followed the intention-to-treat principle.

Results: A total of 140 patients were randomized to IOE (n = 70) or NGT (n = 70). Time to decannulation was shorter with IOE (22.16 ± 1.86 vs. 26.33 ± 1.30 days; between-group difference, 4.17 days; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.90-6.44; p < 0.001; log-rank p = 0.005). The 30-day successful decannulation rate was higher with IOE (65.71% vs. 47.14%; absolute difference, 18.57% points; 95% CI, 2.43-34.71; p = 0.028). At 1 month, the IOE group demonstrated greater improvements in body mass index, serum albumin, serum prealbumin, swallowing function, and swallowing-related quality of life (all p < 0.001). Pharyngeal discomfort was less frequent with IOE (14.06% vs. 34.21%; p = 0.006); no Grade Ⅲ or higher adverse events occurred.

Conclusions: Intermittent oro-esophageal tube feeding shortens time to decannulation and improves nutritional, swallowing, and quality-of-life outcomes compared with nasogastric tube feeding in tracheostomized patients with neurogenic dysphagia.

item.title: Crit Care: Understanding cerebral autoregulation and cerebrovascular reactivity: mechanistic perspectives and clinical insights from TBI
item.description:
Cerebrovascular reactivity and cerebral blood flow autoregulation are critical determinants of brain homeostasis but are often conflated in clinical practice. Although these constructs are closely related and arise from vascular responses to vasoactive stimuli, they reflect distinct physiological responses and measurement approaches: autoregulation is assessed through changes in cerebral blood flow, and pressure reactivity through changes in cerebral blood volume. A fundamental clinical challenge is that the full autoregulatory curve is rarely observable in an individual patient at a single point in time; consequently, isolated measurements from classical assessments or continuous indices such as the pressure reactivity index (PRx), mean flow index (Mx), and arterial mean flow index (Mxa) are each associated with different components of cerebrovascular physiology, providing only partial views of cerebrovascular function and frequently yielding apparently conflicting results. This Review addresses a central clinical question: can multimodal neuromonitoring help determine where a patient is operating on the autoregulatory curve? We synthesise current understanding of the physiological relationships among cerebral perfusion pressure, cerebral blood flow, and cerebral blood volume, and examine the mechanisms underlying divergent autoregulatory index behaviour. By integrating mechanistic physiological schematics and representative clinical cases, we propose an objective educational framework that links classical cerebrovascular physiology with contemporary bedside monitoring. Within this framework, six conceptual physiological zones are delineated. These zones demonstrate how variations in vascular tone, intracranial compliance, and critical closing pressure shape autoregulatory responses generate differing patterns in PRx, Mx, and Mxa. Fully defining a patient's complex cerebrovascular state requires looking beyond any single parameter. Together, PRx, Mx, and Mxa provide complementary information, where discordant findings may represent distinct physiological mechanisms rather than measurement error. Interpreting these indices together within a mechanistic framework may improve identification of a patient's position along the autoregulatory curve, support more consistent bedside interpretation, and ultimately facilitate personalised cerebral perfusion pressure management.

Results: Thoughts of self-harm or death were associated with high-risk (adjusted prevalence ratio [aPR]=1.13, 95% confidence interval: [1.08-1.19]) and very high-risk alcohol use (aPR=1.31 [1.23-1.39]), as well as moderate AUD (aPR=1.24 [1.08-1.41]) and severe AUD (aPR=1.45 [1.30-1.61]). Suicidal ideation/planning/intent were higher across moderate to very high-risk AUDIT-C categories and in patients reporting symptoms consistent with severe AUD. Suicide-related acute care utilization was associated higher across non-drinking, high-risk, and very high-risk AUDIT-C categories and in patients reporting symptoms consistent with severe AUD.

Conclusion: Among primary care patients who screened positive for depression, the AUDIT-C and Alcohol Symptom Checklist can provide clinically useful information for suicide risk assessment to primary care clinicians. It may be beneficial to jointly implement depression and alcohol screening to help integrate alcohol-focused and suicide prevention efforts in primary care.

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: Day-level mediators of change in a brief motivational intervention for alcohol use and liver health
item.description:
Background: Day-level motivation to limit drinking is theorized to be a proximal mechanism of change in motivational interviewing (MI), but day-level evidence remains limited. This study examined whether brief MI with personalized biobehavioral feedback was associated with changes in daily drinking among adults with alcohol use disorder (AUD), including a subgroup with co-occurring alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD), and whether day-level importance and confidence to limit drinking served as within-person mediators.

Methods: Participants (N = 33; M age = 46.0 [12.55]; 799 day-level observations) completed morning surveys for 28 days, including up to 10 pre-intervention days. Each morning, they reported the prior day's standard drinks and rated that day's importance and confidence to limit drinking on 0-10 scales. Multilevel interrupted time-series models included a pre-intervention slope, an intervention-day level shift, and a post-intervention slope, and tested day-level importance and confidence as mediators of daily drinking outcomes.

Results: Daily drinking declined during the pre-intervention period, with no significant intervention-day shifts or post-intervention trends. The intervention-day shift was associated with higher day-level importance of limiting drinking, and higher-than-usual importance and confidence on a given day were associated with fewer planned and actual drinks and lower odds of any and heavy drinking. The intervention-day shift was associated, indirectly, with lower daily drinking through higher same-day importance.

Conclusions: Intensive longitudinal data supported perceived importance of limiting drinking as a proximal mediator of change in brief AUD/ALD interventions, suggesting that frequent, day-level reinforcement of the personal salience of drinking reduction may be a key intervention target.

item.title: J Emerg Med: Predictors of Technical Difficulty in Emergency Department Ultrasound-Guided Nerve Blocks: A Multicenter NURVE Registry Analysis
item.description:
Background: Ultrasound-guided nerve blocks (UGNBs) are increasingly used in emergency departments (EDs), but factors associated with technical difficulty remain poorly characterized.

Objectives: To characterize the frequency of technical difficulty during ED UGNBs and explore patient-, provider-, and block-level factors associated with difficult procedures.

Methods: We performed a retrospective analysis of the multicenter National Ultrasound-guided neRVE (NURVE) Registry, including UGNBs performed at 11 U.S. EDs from January 2022 through December 2023. This interval was selected to capture the complete initial two-year period of NURVE Registry data collection. Technical difficulty was defined by operator self-report using a standardized registry question. Mixed-effects logistic regression with institution as a random intercept was used to evaluate factors associated with technical difficulty.

Results: Among 1725 UGNBs included in the analysis, 82 (4.8%) were reported as technically difficult. In unadjusted analyses, technical difficulty was more common among patients with obesity and differed by block group. In mixed-effects regression, body mass index (BMI) ≥ 30 kg/m² was independently associated with increased odds of technical difficulty compared with BMI 18.5-24.9 kg/m² (odds ratio [OR] 2.94, 95% confidence intervals [CI] 1.58-5.47). Compared with fascia iliaca/femoral region blocks, truncal plane blocks (OR 0.20, 95% CI 0.05-0.87), distal upper-extremity blocks (OR 0.12, 95% CI 0.02-0.94), and distal lower-extremity blocks (OR 0.32, 95% CI 0.10-0.99) were associated with lower odds of technical difficulty. Provider role and prior procedural experience were not significantly associated with difficulty in unadjusted analyses.

Conclusions: Technical difficulty during ED UGNBs was uncommon. Obesity was the most consistent predictor of procedural difficulty, while block-group associations were more modest and influenced by site-level factors. These findings may help inform procedural planning and UGNB training initiatives.

item.title: J Emerg Med: Developing a Model for Hospital Staff Preparedness in Patient Evacuation During Disasters: A Mixed-Methods Study
item.description:
Background: Hospital staff preparedness for patient evacuation during disasters is a component of healthcare resilience. Current protocols may lack evidence-based foundations and tend to rely on static, checklist-driven approaches. Competency-based models have been proposed as an alternative, but empirical evidence supporting their effectiveness is limited.

Objectives: This study aimed to develop a model for hospital evacuation readiness, grounded in global evidence and local expertise.

Methods: An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was conducted in Iran (2023-2025) across five phases: 1) systematic review; 2) qualitative interviews with hospital staff; 3) data integration and expert refinement using a Modified Nominal Group Technique; 4) Delphi consensus validation with specialists; and 5) final model design. The model was developed as a theoretical framework; empirical testing of its effectiveness was beyond the study's scope.

Results: Of 52 initially identified components, 50 were validated through Delphi consensus. The framework identifies five domains: individual factors; education and empowerment; resources; evacuation processes; and communication and coordination. The model introduces practical elements such as stress-tested drills, preemptive resource mapping, and structured near-miss learning.

Conclusions: This research proposes a reconceptualization of evacuation preparedness as an evolving, competency-driven system. The framework offers hospitals strategies to strengthen training, optimize resources, and institutionalize near-miss learning. However, its effectiveness compared with static approaches remains theoretical and requires longitudinal empirical evaluation. Hospitals in resource-constrained regions may particularly benefit from its emphasis on adaptive capacity and low-cost, simulation-based training.

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: Use of anabolic androgenic steroids in a Swedish forensic population: Associations with substance use and criminal convictions
item.description:
Background: The use of anabolic androgenic steroids (AAS) has been associated with adverse psychiatric effects and risk behavior, including increased aggressiveness. The aim of this study was to characterize AAS users in forensic settings and investigate criminal convictions, the use of other substances and sociodemographic factors.

Methods: This descriptive cross-sectional study used Swedish national register data. The study included 3548 men who tested positive for AAS at the National Board of Forensic Medicine between 2010 and 2022. The study population consisted of individuals undergoing forensic toxicological analysis following requests from the police. AAS-positive (AAS-pos) individuals were compared with 6595 men who tested negative for AAS (AAS-neg) and a matched control group of 17,744 men not tested for AAS.

Results: The prevalence of AAS was 35% and testosterone was the most frequently determined AAS. The AAS-pos group had a median of 2.0 rearrests during a two-year follow-up. Concomitant use of illicit and/or licit substances was observed in 50% of the AAS-pos individuals. Cannabis, followed by amphetamines, were the most commonly determined illicit substances across all groups. Compared with the other groups, AAS-pos individuals were more frequently sentenced to imprisonment (p < 0.05). Drug offences showed the largest difference between AAS-pos and AAS-neg individuals. A similar profile was observed for weapons offences.

Conclusion: AAS use in this forensic setting is linked to a pattern of risk behavior characterized by substance use and criminal involvement.
